suppliers.title: Procurement 1 — Suppliers & the Supply Base
suppliers.desc: Suppliers and buying foundations in ZhiftERP: the Supplier doctype walk — groups, country and currency as structural fields, payment terms templates, TIN and withholding per the accountant's ruling, and hold versus disabled; the Supplier Group tree with the management-difference test; contacts, addresses, and the bank-detail control with the call-back verification procedure and the monthly bank-change read; currencies, terms, and the document default chain including foreign-currency exposure; the payables posture — pay on terms, the weekly payment run to verified accounts, and supplier statement reconciliation; the supplier lifecycle — the onboarding gate with document verification, hold with review dates, and retirement; and the seven supplier data reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Supplier record: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module covers the Supplier master and the buying foundations in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: create Supplier records with the full field set including the compliance fields; design the Supplier Group tree; maintain supplier contacts, addresses, and bank details under the change controls; configure currencies and payment terms with the document default chain; operate the payables posture; run the supplier lifecycle from onboarding through hold to retirement; and run the supplier data reads on their cadences.

What a Supplier record is. A Supplier is the register record of a party the business buys from. Every purchasing document — Material Request routing, Request for Quotation, Purchase Order, Purchase Receipt, Purchase Invoice — names a supplier, and pulls its behaviour from that supplier's record: the currency the supplier bills in, the payment terms the business has agreed, the addresses goods ship from and invoices come from, the tax treatment, and the bank account the business pays into. The Supplier record is the buying side's mirror of the Customer record, and the same construction rule applies: documents behave correctly because the master was built correctly.

What reads the Supplier record.

1. The purchasing documents — every transaction in modules 3-7 begins by naming the supplier.
2. The payables ledger — supplier balances, due dates, and the payment schedule all key on the record.
3. The costing machinery — module 2's buying price lists and the landed-cost flow resolve through the supplier.
4. The compliance machinery — withholding tax applicability, TIN records, and the documentation the statutory returns require.
5. The payment run — the bank details on the record are where the business's money goes; for this reason those fields carry the tightest change control in the register (Chapter 4).

Custody. The procurement function operates the records; the owner decides terms postures per the ladder; the accountant owns the payables side, the tax fields, and the withholding rulings; bank-detail changes run the verification procedure without exception; and record creation runs through the onboarding gate (Chapter 7).

Build order. The tree before the records, the records before the documents: the Supplier Group tree designed (Chapter 3); the onboarding gate written (Chapter 7); suppliers created through the gate with contacts, addresses, and verified bank details (Chapters 2, 4); currencies and terms set per the decisions (Chapter 5).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Supplier doctype walk. Chapter 3: the Supplier Group tree. Chapter 4: contacts, addresses, and bank details. Chapter 5: currencies, terms, and the default chain. Chapter 6: the payables posture. Chapter 7: the supplier lifecycle and the data reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Supplier doctype
lessons.html:
Open Supplier (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Supplier Name. The registered legal name per the naming convention — the name on the supplier's own invoices and registration documents, consistently formatted. The name prints on Purchase Orders and appears on every payables report; it is entered once, from documents, at the gate.

2. Supplier Group. The classification from Chapter 3's tree — pharmaceutical manufacturers, importers and trading houses, equipment vendors, service providers. The group is a working field: buying defaults can derive from it, the spend reports aggregate by it, and the approval postures the policy sets can reference it.

3. Supplier Type and Country. Company or Individual, and the supplier's country. The country field matters operationally: it signals the currency and import questions Chapter 5 covers, and it drives which compliance documentation the gate requires — a domestic manufacturer and a foreign manufacturer carry different verification sets.

4. Billing Currency. The currency the supplier invoices in. This field sets the currency of every document raised on the supplier, and it is a structural decision: a supplier billing in a foreign currency exposes the business to exchange movements between order and payment, which the terms decision (Chapter 5) must account for.

5. Default Price List (buying). The buying price list the supplier's documents pre-fill from — module 2 covers the buying lists. The resolution chain mirrors the selling side: the supplier's own default, else the group's, else the buying default.

6. Payment Terms Template. The terms the business has agreed with this supplier — the template that computes due dates on every Purchase Invoice (Chapter 6). Set from the negotiated agreement, not assumed.

7. Tax and compliance fields. Per the accountant's ruling table:

1. The supplier's TIN — required for the statutory documentation of purchases and the withholding-tax records.
2. Withholding tax applicability — whether payments to this supplier attract withholding under the rules the accountant maintains (service suppliers commonly do; goods suppliers per the ruling), and at which category. The field carries the accountant's ruling; the payment machinery applies it; the operator neither decides nor overrides it.
3. Tax category where the site uses category-based purchase tax rules.

8. Hold and Disabled. Two distinct instruments: Hold suspends new business with a live supplier (quality failures, disputes) while history and open items remain workable — the hold type controls what is blocked (invoices, payments, or all); Disabled retires the record at zero balance when the relationship ends. Suppliers are never deleted; document history references every supplier that ever traded.

Verification per record. The name from documents; the group and country correct; the currency as the supplier actually bills; terms per the agreement; TIN and withholding per the ruling; the primary contact, address, and verified bank details attached (Chapter 4).

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Supplier Group tree
lessons.html:
One tree classifies the supply base. This chapter is its design procedure.

1. What the tree answers. The Supplier Group answers the commercial question: what kind of supply is this? The classes are the kinds of supply the business manages differently — different terms postures, different approval sensitivity, different reads. For a pharmaceutical distributor: manufacturers (the direct factory relationships), importers and trading houses (the intermediary channel), equipment vendors, logistics and transport, and service providers (professional and facility services). A class with no management difference is a report filter, not a group.

2. The design procedure. On paper first, per the standing tree rules:

1. List the supply classes the business actually treats differently. The test questions: do these suppliers carry different payment postures? Different compliance requirements (withholding on services)? Different quality regimes (manufacturers carry product-quality obligations that service providers do not)? Different spend review?
2. Three levels or fewer — the root, the major classes, and subdivisions only where management genuinely differs (manufacturers split domestic and foreign where the terms and compliance sets differ, which for an importing distributor they do).
3. Wire the defaults — where a class shares a terms posture or price list, set it at the group so new members inherit, and record the wiring in the convention.

3. The classification's uses, stated.

1. Spend analysis — purchases by group is the first cut of every spend review: what the business spends on manufacturers versus intermediaries versus services is a structural figure the owner reads quarterly.
2. Policy application — the procurement policy's rules reference groups: which classes require competitive quotes (module 4), which carry the scorecard regime (module 8), which attract withholding review.
3. Risk reading — concentration by group (one manufacturer carrying most of a class's volume) is a supply-risk figure the quarterly review compiles.

4. The change discipline. The tree changes by decision with the reason recorded; reclassifying a supplier is an ordinary edit with a note; restructuring is a governed event. The rule is identical to the selling side because the cost is identical: every new node fragments the history of the reports that aggregate on it.

5. The classification read — quarterly. Suppliers per group sampled against the definitions; the importer that became a manufacturer's direct channel regrouped; near-empty groups with no management difference flagged for merge at the structural review. The read rides the same quarterly calendar as the rest of the programme's structure reviews.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Contacts, addresses, and bank details
lessons.html:
The people, places, and payment destinations of supply. The third of these carries the register's tightest control.

1. Contacts. One Contact record per person, linked to the supplier:

1. The sales contact — the supplier's person who receives Purchase Orders and answers availability questions: the primary contact, because a Purchase Order sent to a generic address is an order nobody at the supplier owns.
2. The accounts contact — the supplier's receivables person: where remittance advices go and where statement reconciliations are conducted.
3. The quality and escalation contacts where the class requires them (manufacturers carry a quality contact for the module 6 receiving disputes and module 8 scorecard conversations).

2. Addresses. One Address record per physical location, linked and flagged: the billing address (where the supplier invoices from — it prints on the compliance records) and the shipping origin addresses where the business arranges collection or tracks origin. Multi-site suppliers (a manufacturer despatching from two plants) carry an address per site, titled per the convention.

3. Bank details — the controlled fields. The supplier's bank account is where the business's money goes, and supplier-bank-detail fraud — an emailed instruction to change the account, followed by payments to the fraudster — is among the most common and expensive frauds in payables. The register therefore treats these fields under a written control:

1. Entry at the gate — bank details enter from the supplier's official documentation and are verified by the call-back procedure: a call to the supplier's known number (the number from the register, never the number on the instruction) confirming the account name, number, and bank, with the verification recorded — who called, whom they spoke to, when.
2. Changes run the same verification, without exception — an emailed change instruction is precisely the fraud pattern; the change is not entered until the call-back to the known contact confirms it. Urgency in the instruction raises suspicion rather than lowering the control.
3. Write permission — bank fields are writable by the named roles only, per the matrix; every change is system-logged.
4. The bank-change read — monthly — every bank-detail change in the month, with who changed it and the verification record attached. A change without its verification is treated as a live incident: payments to the account stop until the verification completes.

4. Hygiene. Quarterly, riding the standing calendar: primary contacts confirmed for the top suppliers by spend; addresses sampled against recent documents; leavers replaced. The payables function surfaces dead contacts naturally — a remittance advice that bounces is a hygiene finding routed to the read.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Currencies, terms, and the default chain
lessons.html:
Three master fields — currency, payment terms, price list — flow from the Supplier record onto every purchasing document. This chapter is the chain and the two decisions riding it.

1. The default chain. At document creation, the supplier's fields pre-fill the document: the billing currency sets the document currency; the payment terms template sets the schedule the invoice will compute due dates from; the price list supplies the expected rates (module 2). The chain is wired once, verified at the gate's first-document check, and the operator's job at document time is verification, not composition — the same rule as the selling side.

2. Foreign-currency suppliers. A supplier billing in a foreign currency introduces exchange exposure: the naira cost of the commitment moves between order, receipt, and payment as the rate moves. The operational rules:

1. The document carries the supplier's currency and the exchange rate at posting, per the rate source the Accounts track configures; the ledger carries both the foreign amount and the naira value.
2. The exposure is priced at commitment — the module 4 order decision accounts for the exposure window (order to payment), and the terms decision below interacts with it: longer terms on a foreign-currency supplier lengthen the exposure window.
3. Revaluation and settlement differences are the accountant's territory — the Accounts track's period procedures; the procurement obligation is documents with honest dates and correct currencies so those procedures compute from true records.

3. The terms decision. Payment terms with a supplier are a negotiated asset: 30-day terms mean the business holds its cash thirty days longer per purchase cycle, and the working-capital value of that holding is real and computable. The postures:

1. Terms are negotiated at onboarding and renegotiated at review — per the ladder: the standard ask per class, the owner's decision on strategic relationships.
2. Terms are recorded as templates (Chapter 2) — the template computes every invoice's due date; terms that exist only in conversation compute nothing.
3. Early-payment discounts are evaluated, not reflexively taken or ignored — a discount for early settlement is priced against the working-capital cost per the accountant's arithmetic, and the decision per supplier is recorded.

4. The chain read — quarterly. A sample per supplier class: a draft document per supplier confirming the currency, terms, and list pre-fill as the register states; discrepancies corrected at the register. The read is cheap and it is the difference between a register that describes the supply base and one that merely lists it.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — The payables posture
lessons.html:
Payables are managed deliberately, as receivables are on the selling side. This chapter is the posture — the decisions and reads that govern what the business owes.

1. The payables position. The Accounts Payable report: open Purchase Invoices per supplier, bucketed by age against due date. The figures depend on the disciplines this track builds: invoices posted from documents (module 7), due dates from templates (Chapter 5), payments allocated per remittances. The position is read weekly by the payables function and monthly by the owner with the payables summary.

2. Paying on terms. The standing posture is stated plainly: the business pays on the due date — neither habitually early nor habitually late.

1. Not habitually early, because terms were negotiated for their working-capital value and paying early returns that value unasked; early payment is a decision (a priced discount, a strategic relationship gesture), not a default.
2. Not habitually late, because lateness is priced by suppliers into the next negotiation, surfaces as supply risk (the manufacturer that ships the reliable payer first), and on strategic relationships costs more than the cash timing gains. The scorecard conversation (module 8) runs in both directions; suppliers score their customers too, informally and consequentially.

3. The payment run. Payments run on a cadence (weekly per the policy), from the due list:

1. The run's list — invoices due in the window, verified (three-way matched per module 7), with withholding computed per the rulings.
2. The approvals — the run is approved per the matrix's bands; individual off-run payments are exceptions with named approval.
3. The execution — payments to the register's verified bank details only (Chapter 4's control closing its loop here); remittance advices to the supplier's accounts contact.

4. Supplier statement reconciliation. The mirror of the selling side's statement cycle, run from the receiving end: the supplier's statement against the business's ledger, monthly for the top suppliers by spend, differences traced through the document references — the missing invoice, the unallocated payment, the disputed receipt — and resolved at the document that differs. A supplier account that reconciles monthly never produces the year-end investigation backlog of one that does not; the read's cost is minutes per account.

5. The payables summary — monthly. The owner's page: total payables, due profile for the coming weeks (the cash requirement), overdue value with reasons, withholding remitted and pending, and the terms map — average terms held per class against the policy's targets. One page, filed with the monthly review.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The supplier lifecycle and the data reads
lessons.html:
Suppliers are vetted in, held when trouble surfaces, and retired when relationships end. This chapter is the lifecycle and the standing reads.

1. The onboarding gate. Suppliers enter the register by gate, in order:

1. The duplicate check first — the register searched by name fragments, TIN, phone, and bank account before creation. A duplicate supplier splits spend history and payables across records and defeats the concentration reads.
2. Verification against documents — the registration documents (CAC registration for Nigerian companies), the TIN, and the trading address verified against official documentation; for foreign suppliers, the equivalent registration set per the compliance owner's checklist. The verification protects against both error and the fictitious-supplier fraud pattern.
3. Bank details by the call-back procedure (Chapter 4) — entered from official documentation, verified to the known number, recorded.
4. Classification — group per the tree's definitions.
5. Terms and currency per the decisions — the negotiated terms as a template; the billing currency confirmed.
6. Compliance fields per the ruling — TIN recorded; withholding applicability ruled by the accountant.
7. The first-document check — a draft Purchase Order confirming the pre-fill chain; deleted after reading.

2. Hold. The instrument for live trouble: quality failures under investigation, unresolved disputes, a failed verification. The hold enters with its reason and its type (blocking new orders, invoices, payments, or all per the case), the supplier is informed where the policy says so, and the hold is reviewed on a stated date — a hold without a review date becomes a forgotten relationship rather than a managed one. Release is a decision recorded with what resolved.

3. Retirement. At relationship end: open items settled to zero, the record Disabled with the reason, the history preserved. The annual pass sweeps dormant suppliers (no documents across the policy window) into the retirement decision — a dormant record with live bank details and open permissions is exposure with no relationship attached.

4. The supplier data reads, consolidated.

1. The bank-change read — monthly (Chapter 4): every change against its verification; unverified changes treated as incidents.
2. The duplicate-candidate read — monthly: near-identical names, shared TINs or bank accounts across records — a shared bank account across two supplier records is a fraud indicator investigated, not merely merged.
3. The classification read — quarterly (Chapter 3).
4. The chain read — quarterly (Chapter 5).
5. The hygiene read — quarterly (Chapter 4).
6. The dormancy read — quarterly: candidates for retirement; holds past their review dates.
7. The concentration read — quarterly: spend share by supplier within each group — the single-source classes and the one-supplier dependencies listed for the owner's risk review, with the figures and the suppliers named.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: HealthTrade's supply base
lessons.html:
This chapter applies Chapters 2-7 to the standing case: the supply base behind the selling and inventory operations the other tracks built. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

The base. HealthTrade's purchasing concentrates on: two local pharmaceutical manufacturers — Emzor and a second domestic manufacturer — supplying the core pharmaceutical range in naira; one Indian manufacturer supplying selected generics, billing in US dollars; and a European equipment vendor for the retail-equipment line, billing in euros. The register therefore carries three currencies, and the base's design places the two channels the tree distinguishes — domestic manufacturers and foreign manufacturers — under different compliance sets.

Step 1 — the tree (Chapter 3). The Supplier Group tree: Manufacturers (Domestic, Foreign), Importers & Trading Houses, Equipment Vendors, Logistics, Services. Group defaults wire the domestic manufacturers' standard terms posture; the Services group carries the withholding flag per the accountant's ruling table.

Step 2 — the gate runs four times (Chapter 7). Each supplier onboards through the full gate: duplicate checks clean; CAC and TIN verification for the domestic pair; the foreign registration sets for the Indian manufacturer and the equipment vendor per the compliance checklist; bank details entered from official documentation and verified by call-back to known numbers, each verification recorded. The first-document checks confirm the pre-fill chains.

Step 3 — currencies and terms (Chapter 5). Emzor and the second domestic manufacturer bill in naira on 30-day terms — negotiated at onboarding, recorded as the template, the working-capital value noted in the decision file. The Indian manufacturer bills in US dollars; the terms decision records the exposure window explicitly (order to payment across the import lead time), and the order sizing in module 5 will account for it. The equipment vendor bills in euros on the project-payment terms its class carries.

Step 4 — the payables posture installs (Chapter 6). The weekly payment run stands up from the due list; the pay-on-terms posture is written into the policy; supplier statement reconciliation begins monthly with the two domestic manufacturers (the top of the spend concentration). The first monthly payables summary compiles: the due profile, the terms map, and a clean bank-change read.

Step 5 — the reads return their first findings (Chapter 7). The duplicate-candidate read flags a legacy trading-house record with the same TIN as a retired importer — merged per the remediation with the documents re-pointed. The concentration read states the structural figure the owner already suspected: the domestic pharmaceutical class concentrates heavily on Emzor — recorded with the figures for the risk review, where the second manufacturer's range overlap becomes the mitigation conversation. The first quarter closes with the register verified, the chains confirmed, and every read filed.

The register evidence. The gate files hold the verifications; the decision files hold the terms with their reasoning; the bank-change read holds its clean month; the concentration read holds the risk figure with names. The supply base is answerable from its files, per the standing standard, before a single Purchase Order ships — which is the state module 3's demand machinery builds on.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in supplier foundations, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the unverified bank change. Symptom: bank details changed on an emailed instruction; payments to an account nobody verified; the fraud discovered at the supplier's overdue call. Correction: payments stopped, the incident procedure run, recovery attempted through the bank. Prevention: the call-back procedure without exception, write permission per the matrix, and the monthly bank-change read.

Error 2 — the duplicate supplier. Symptom: one supplier's spend and balance split across records; concentration reads understated; two records sharing one bank account. Correction: investigated first (the shared account may be the fraud indicator), then merged per the remediation. Prevention: the gate's duplicate check across name, TIN, phone, and bank account.

Error 3 — terms that exist only in conversation. Symptom: due dates improvised per invoice; the negotiated 30 days neither enforced nor measured; the working-capital value leaking. Correction: templates applied from the decision files. Prevention: every negotiated term recorded as a template at the gate.

Error 4 — the habitual posture. Symptom: paying everything early (the negotiated value returned unasked) or everything late (supply risk and priced-in lateness). Correction: the payment run rebuilt on the due list; exceptions become decisions. Prevention: the pay-on-terms posture and the weekly run.

Error 5 — the unmanaged hold. Symptom: suppliers held without review dates; relationships frozen by inattention; or trouble suppliers never held at all, with new orders flowing through open disputes. Correction: holds reviewed and resolved by decision. Prevention: every hold with a reason, a type, and a review date.

Error 6 — the fictitious supplier. Symptom: a record created without document verification; invoices approved against no real supply; the classic payables fraud. Correction: the incident procedure, the record frozen, the approval chain examined. Prevention: the gate's document verification, the segregation the matrix enforces between record creation and payment approval, and the duplicate read's bank-account matching.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the Supplier walk including the compliance fields and the hold-versus-disabled distinction; design the tree with the management-difference test; operate contacts, addresses, and the bank-detail control with the call-back procedure; state the default chain and the foreign-currency rules; run the payables posture — pay on terms, the run, statement reconciliation; run the gate, hold, and retirement; and run the seven data reads.

Module rule 1: every purchasing document stands on its Supplier record — created through the gate with documents verified and bank details confirmed by call-back, classified by the tree, carrying negotiated terms as templates and the supplier's true currency, paid on terms to verified accounts only, and kept true by the scheduled reads. Module 2 covers items and buying costs.

items_costs.title: Procurement 2 — Purchase Items, Costs & UOMs
items_costs.desc: Purchase items, units, costs, and planning in ZhiftERP: the buying section on the one register record with Is Purchase Item and the one-record principle; purchase units with physically verified factors, the rate-and-unit pairing rule, and governed pack-size changes; buying price lists with sourced rates and the changes and completeness reads; the three figures called cost — quoted, invoiced, and landed — with their sources, uses, and the margin vocabulary rule; the planning fields — measured lead times, costed safety stock, reorder parameters, and supplier constraints; reading the last purchase rate within its boundaries and the monthly price trend read with the selling-review hand-off; and landed-cost thinking — the consignment worksheet, the landed comparison rule, container arithmetic, and the worksheet-versus-actual reconciliation.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The item's buying side: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module covers purchase items, units, costs, and planning fields in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the item's buying field set on the one register record; operate purchase units of measure with their conversions; maintain buying price lists and supplier rates; distinguish the three figures called cost and use each correctly; complete the planning fields that drive replenishment; read the last purchase rate and the price trend; and compute in landed-cost terms for imported goods.

One record, both sides of trade. The Item is one record serving selling and buying. The Selling track completed the commercial section; this module completes the buying section — how the item is purchased, in what units, from which suppliers, at what agreed rates, with what planning parameters. The one-record principle is restated because the most common structural error on the buying side is its violation: a separate buying item is never created for a product the register already holds. A PARA-500-BUY record beside PARA-500 splits the item's stock, cost history, and planning arithmetic into two half-records, each wrong; the buying section of the existing record is completed instead, through the item gate the Inventory track defined.

What buying reads from the Item.

1. Is Purchase Item — the flag that admits the item to purchasing documents: the buying mirror of the selling flag, and the first check when an item will not appear on a Purchase Order.
2. The purchase units — the default purchase unit and the conversion table (Chapter 2): what quantity means on a buying document.
3. The rates — through the buying price lists and supplier-specific prices (Chapter 3), plus the system-maintained last purchase rate (Chapter 6).
4. The planning fields — lead time, safety stock, reorder levels (Chapter 5): the parameters module 3's demand machinery computes from.
5. The valuation tie — what the item truly costs is the valuation question the Inventory track's module 5 owns; this module supplies its inputs (Chapters 4, 7).

Custody. The procurement function maintains the buying section; supplier rates change by the governed update, mirroring the selling side; planning fields change by decision with the replenishment review; and the standing rule: a cost is a defined figure with a source — the quoted rate, the invoiced rate, and the landed valuation are three different numbers, named correctly on every document and decision.

Module contents. Chapter 2: purchase units. Chapter 3: buying price lists. Chapter 4: the three cost figures. Chapter 5: the planning fields. Chapter 6: reading purchase prices. Chapter 7: landed-cost thinking. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Purchase units and the conversion arithmetic
lessons.html:
Suppliers sell in cartons, drums, and pallets; stock counts in units. This chapter runs the unit machinery inbound.

1. The Default Purchase UOM. On the Item's purchasing section: the unit buying documents pre-fill with — set to how the item is normally bought (the carton for the standing pharmaceutical case), while stock continues to count in the stock unit. Any converted unit can be selected per document row; the default is the normal case, not a restriction.

2. The conversion table, inbound. The same table the Selling track verified (Carton-12 = 12 units) serves buying, and the same rules apply with the inbound consequences stated:

1. Factors come from the physical product, verified at the register. On the inbound side, the supplier's carton contents are counted at first receipt and at any pack-size change — the supplier's catalogue is the claim; the count is the verification.
2. A wrong factor mis-posts every receipt. The receipt entered in cartons converts to stock units by the factor: a factor of 12 where the physical carton holds 10 overstates stock by a fifth on every receipt and understates unit cost by the same proportion — both errors silent until a count or a margin review surfaces them.
3. The rate-and-unit pairing rule. A rate belongs to a unit: ₦9,600 per carton and ₦800 per unit are the same price stated twice, and every document row is read as quantity-unit-rate together. The receiving discipline (module 6) names this pairing as its first check, because the carton-rate-entered-on-a-unit-line receipt is the classic inbound costing error — the Inventory track's remediation cases include exactly this pattern.

3. Pack-size changes. A supplier changing carton contents is a governed, dated change: the factor updates, the carton-denominated rates update in the same decision (the pairing rule applied to maintenance), and open Purchase Orders in the old pack size are reviewed — an order for 100 old cartons received against new cartons mis-counts by the pack difference unless the order is amended first.

4. The purchase-unit read — quarterly. Riding the item lifecycle reads: factors sampled against physical cartons for the top-purchased items; rate-unit pairings sampled on the quarter's receipts; items bought in units their table does not carry corrected by adding the decided unit. The read shares its calendar with the selling-side conversion read; one register, both directions confirmed.

Where the unit error actually bites. Not at the order, where a wrong unit is usually obvious from the total, but at the receipt — where a quantity in cartons meets a rate per unit and produces a valuation wrong by twelve. The stock then carries that figure into every margin calculation until somebody notices, and by then it has been sold. The pairing check at both ends exists because the two documents are prepared by different people on different days.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Buying price lists and supplier rates
lessons.html:
The buying side encodes who charges what, so documents fetch agreed rates instead of remembered ones. This chapter is the architecture.

1. The buying Price List. Open Price List > New with the Buying flag: the named context for purchase rates, in its currency. The standing architecture mirrors the selling side's restraint:

1. The standard buying list — the default naira context most domestic purchasing resolves to.
2. Currency lists where suppliers bill in other currencies — the US-dollar list the Indian manufacturer's rates live on, per module 1's currency structure.
3. Additional lists only by decision — the same anti-proliferation rule as selling: every list is a rate set to maintain.

2. Item Prices, buying. One row per item per list (with UOM and validity where used): the agreed rate with the supplier — the negotiated figure from module 4's quotation cycle or module 8's arrangements, entered by the governed update with its source recorded. The rate on the list is a decision with a paper trail: the quotation, the arrangement, or the negotiation file it came from.

3. Supplier-specific rates. Where the site maintains rates per supplier (the supplier's own quoted prices as distinct from a general buying list), the price machinery resolves the supplier's rate onto the supplier's documents. The maintenance rule is unchanged: rates enter from documents (the supplier's quotation or price circular, filed), by the governed update, and the price changes read reconciles the month's changes to their sources.

4. What the buying lists are for. Their operational function, stated:

1. Pre-fill — the Purchase Order draws the agreed rate; the preparer verifies rather than recalls.
2. Variance detection — the invoice-versus-order rate check (module 7's matching) has a reference because the order had one.
3. Negotiation memory — the list states the current agreement; the update files state its history; the module 4 comparison worksheets state the alternatives considered. A price conversation with a supplier is conducted from these records.

5. The buying price reads — monthly. The changes read: every buying Item Price change against its source document, per the fields-move-by-decision pattern. The completeness read: actively purchased items without a current rate on their supplier's context — the gap that forces typed rates on orders, which is the door this architecture closes. Both worked to zero with the update cycle.

Why the buying lists stay few. Every list is a rate set somebody must maintain, and an unmaintained list is worse than no list — it supplies a stale rate with the authority of a record. The temptation is a list per supplier, which multiplies the maintenance by the size of the supply base. Rates that genuinely belong to one supplier belong in that supplier's arrangement, not in a list of their own.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The three figures called cost
lessons.html:
Three different numbers are all called cost. This chapter defines each, names its source, and states what each is for — because confusing them misprices decisions.

1. The quoted rate — what the supplier asks. Source: the supplier's quotation, price circular, or arrangement (modules 4, 8), held on the buying lists. Definition: the agreed or offered price per unit in the supplier's currency, before anything happens. Used for: ordering decisions, comparisons between suppliers, and the Purchase Order's rate. Not used for: valuing stock or computing margin — the quoted rate omits everything between the supplier's gate and the business's shelf.

2. The invoiced rate — what the supplier charges. Source: the Purchase Invoice (module 7). Definition: the price actually billed per unit, which the matching discipline compares to the order's quoted rate — a variance is a finding, not a correction to wave through. Used for: the payables liability, the matching control, and the price trend (Chapter 6). The invoiced rate is the commercial truth of one transaction; it is still not the shelf cost.

3. The landed valuation — what the shelf cost is. Source: the stock ledger, per the Inventory track's module 5: the receipt's rate plus the capitalised acquisition costs — freight, clearing, duties, insurance — attached through the Landed Cost Voucher where they apply (Chapter 7). Definition: the per-unit value at which stock is carried and consumed — the figure Moving Average or FIFO maintains. Used for: margin arithmetic, pricing reviews (the selling side's price decisions read this figure), dead-stock and markdown decisions, and every valuation report. This is the only one of the three figures that may be called cost in a margin sentence.

4. The discipline, applied.

1. On documents — the Purchase Order carries the quoted rate; the invoice carries the invoiced rate; the stock ledger carries the valuation. No document's figure is typed over to match another; differences route through their controls (matching, Landed Cost Vouchers, the variance reads).
2. In decisions — a selling-price review that reads the quoted rate instead of the landed valuation understates cost by the acquisition layer and overstates margin by the same amount; on imported lines the gap is material (Chapter 7 quantifies it). The decision rule: margin sentences use the landed valuation; negotiation sentences use the quoted and invoiced rates.
3. In conversation — the register's vocabulary names which figure is meant. The question what does this item cost receives a counter-question — for buying, for billing, or on the shelf — until the register's users ask it precisely themselves.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The planning fields
lessons.html:
The item master carries the parameters replenishment computes from. This chapter is each field, its honest value, and its review.

1. Lead Time Days. Definition: the days from placing the order to stock being available for sale — order processing, the supplier's fulfilment, transit, receiving, and quality release, end to end. The honest value is measured, not hoped: the actual order-to-availability history per supplier (module 8's on-time data feeds it). Domestic manufacturers and the Indian import line carry very different figures, and each item's field carries its own supplier reality. Every reorder computation multiplies demand by this figure; an optimistic lead time is a stock-out generator by arithmetic.

2. Safety Stock. Definition: the buffer held against demand and supply variability — the quantity intended to remain when the replenishment arrives on time. Set per the policy's method (days-of-sales for the standing case), higher where lead times are long or variable (the import line) and lower where replenishment is fast. Safety stock is a costed decision: it is money held on shelves deliberately, sized by the variability it protects against, and reviewed rather than ratcheted.

3. Reorder Level and Reorder Quantity. The item-warehouse reorder table the Inventory track's module 6 operates: the level (demand over lead time plus safety stock) and the quantity per the ordering policy (the economic batch, the supplier's minimums, the carton multiples). This module's contribution is the inputs' honesty — the level computes from Chapter 5.1 and 5.2's figures, and the quantity respects the purchase unit's realities (orders in carton multiples per Chapter 2).

4. Minimum Order Quantity and the supplier constraints. The item's MOQ field where suppliers impose one, and the practical constraints the ordering policy records: the supplier's carton or pallet multiples, the price-break thresholds (the module 4 quotations state them), and the import line's container arithmetic (Chapter 7). Replenishment quantities are shaped by these constraints deliberately — the reorder review documents where a constraint forces ordering above the computed need, because that excess is a costed consequence of the supply structure, visible rather than accidental.

5. The planning review — with the reorder review's cadence. The fields against reality: lead times re-measured from the period's receipts (the module 8 on-time read supplies the actuals); safety stock against the period's stock-outs and excesses; reorder parameters against what the period actually demanded. Fields move by decision at the review, dated — a planning field changed mid-period by an unrecorded edit is the configuration drift the change read catches.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Reading purchase prices: the last purchase rate and the trend
lessons.html:
The system records what the business actually paid. This chapter is the reading of that record — and the boundaries of its use.

1. Last Purchase Rate. Maintained automatically: the rate on the item's most recent purchase, per unit. Its uses:

1. The reasonableness check — the order preparer sees the new rate against the last: a movement is verified against its cause (a known price change, a currency movement, a pack-size change) before the order proceeds.
2. The quick answer — what the business last paid, without opening the ledger.

2. What the last purchase rate is not. The boundaries, stated:

1. Not the valuation — stock on the shelf carries the method's figure (Moving Average across receipts, or FIFO's layers), not the latest rate; the two diverge whenever prices move, and margin arithmetic uses the valuation (Chapter 4's rule).
2. Not the agreed rate — the buying list states the current agreement; the last rate states the last transaction. Where they differ, the difference is a question: an unapplied price change, a one-off premium, or an error the matching read should have caught.
3. Not a pricing authority — a Purchase Order rate is justified by its list or its quotation, not by repetition of the last rate; repetition compounds any error in it.

3. The price trend read — monthly. Purchase rates per item across periods, for the top items by spend:

1. The movement list — items whose rate moved beyond the threshold, each with its explanation written (the supplier's increase and its notice, the currency movement on import lines, a pack-size change misread as a price change — the pairing rule's audit).
2. The margin hand-off — confirmed cost increases route to the selling side's pricing review (the module 2 governed update on the selling lists), because a cost increase absorbed silently is a margin decrease decided by nobody.
3. The negotiation file — the trend per supplier accumulates as the material of the module 8 review conversations: what moved, when, with what notice, against what market reference where one exists.

4. The variance connection. The trend read works alongside module 7's matching: matching catches the single invoice that disagrees with its order; the trend catches the drift that arrives in small agreed steps. Both file monthly, and together they are the buying side's price evidence — the record every negotiation and every review draws on.

What to do when the last purchase rate has no history behind it. A first purchase, a returning line, an item whose last buy was two years ago — in each case the check has nothing to compare against, and the answer is not to skip it but to substitute a reference: the arrangement rate, the quoted rate from the cycle, or a comparable item's movement. A rate with nothing to check it against is exactly the rate most worth a second look before it enters the valuation.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Landed-cost thinking
lessons.html:
For imported goods, the factory price is the beginning of the cost, not the cost. This chapter is the landed computation and its operational rules.

1. The landed cost, defined. The per-unit value of imported stock on the shelf: the supplier's invoice value plus every cost incurred to bring the goods to usable condition and location — international freight, marine insurance, customs duties and levies, clearing agent charges, port and terminal charges, local haulage — capitalised into the stock's valuation rather than expensed. The Inventory track's module 5 covered the mechanism (the Landed Cost Voucher attaching costs to a receipt and re-rating its stock); this chapter is the buying-side computation and habits.

2. The landed worksheet. Per import consignment, the standing worksheet computes the expected landed cost before commitment:

1. The goods value — the supplier's price in its currency, converted at the planning rate.
2. The acquisition layer — freight per the forwarder's quote; insurance per the policy's rate; duties per the tariff classification the clearing agent confirms (the classification is confirmed in advance, because a tariff surprise at the port is a landed-cost surprise after commitment); clearing, port, and haulage per the standing rates.
3. The per-unit result — the consignment's total landed cost divided over its units: the figure the ordering decision, and later the selling-price review, actually needs.

3. The comparison rule. Suppliers are compared landed, never ex-works: the domestic manufacturer's naira rate and the Indian manufacturer's dollar rate are incomparable until both are stated as naira-per-unit-on-the-shelf. The module 4 quotation comparisons apply this rule as procedure — the comparison worksheet carries a landed column, and the decision minutes record landed figures.

4. Consignment arithmetic. The import line's quantities are shaped by the consignment: freight and clearing are substantially fixed per shipment, so the per-unit acquisition layer falls as the consignment fills — the container arithmetic that makes import ordering a batch decision rather than a reorder-point decision alone. The planning consequence (Chapter 5): import items order in consignment-sized batches on the import calendar, with safety stock covering the longer, lumpier cycle.

5. After arrival: the reconciliation. The worksheet's expected figures reconcile to actuals when the consignment lands: the Landed Cost Voucher applies the actual charges to the receipt (the Inventory mechanism), and the worksheet-versus-actual comparison files with the consignment — the recurring differences (a forwarder consistently above quote, a duty line misclassified) are the findings the next consignment's worksheet corrects. The read keeps the planning figures honest, and it is the difference between an import operation that knows its costs and one that discovers them.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: PARA-500's buying architecture
lessons.html:
This chapter completes the record whose selling side the Selling track built. Configuration values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the one record confirmed (Chapter 1). PARA-500 — Paracetamol 500mg Tablets — already exists in the register with its selling section complete. The buying section completes on the same record: Is Purchase Item on; the buying defaults per the accountant's design. The rejected alternative is recorded in the register note: no PARA-500-BUY record — a second record would split stock, cost history, and planning into two half-records.

Step 2 — the purchase units (Chapter 2). Default Purchase UOM: Carton-12 — Emzor supplies in cartons of twelve. The factor was verified physically at first receipt (the Inventory track's register discipline); the pairing rule files with the register: the carton rate ₦9,600 and the unit rate ₦800 are one price, and every order and receipt row is read quantity-unit-rate together.

Step 3 — the buying rates (Chapter 3). The standard buying list carries PARA-500 at ₦9,600 per Carton-12, entered by the governed update with its source: the Emzor arrangement from the module 4 cycle. The completeness read confirms every actively purchased item on the range carries its current rate; the changes read's first month reconciles to sources exactly.

Step 4 — the three costs stated (Chapter 4). For PARA-500 the three figures are written into the register note as the vocabulary example: the quoted rate ₦9,600 per carton (the Emzor agreement); the invoiced rate as billed and matched per delivery; the landed valuation — for this domestic line, effectively the receipt rate, since the acquisition layer is the supplier's included delivery. The contrast case is the Indian manufacturer's generic line, where the worksheet shows the dollar goods value carrying a material acquisition layer — freight, duty, clearing — before it becomes a shelf figure, and where a selling-price review reading the quoted dollar rate instead of the landed naira figure would overstate margin on every unit.

Step 5 — the planning fields (Chapter 5). PARA-500's fields enter from measured reality: the domestic lead time from Emzor's actual order-to-availability history; safety stock per the days-of-sales policy at the item's velocity; the reorder row per warehouse with the quantity in carton multiples. The import generics carry their own figures: the long lead time measured across the consignment cycle, the larger safety stock the variability requires, and consignment-batch ordering per Chapter 7's arithmetic.

Step 6 — the first trend read (Chapter 6). Month one's read lists two movements: a notified Emzor increase on one line (explanation written; routed to the selling pricing review — the governed update runs on the selling list the same week), and an apparent jump on an import line that the pairing audit resolves as a pack-size change, not a price change — the factor and rates corrected together per Chapter 2's rule. Both findings file; neither is absorbed silently.

The architecture evidence. One record with both sides complete; verified units with the pairing rule; rates with sources; the three costs named; planning fields from measured figures; the trend read operating. Module 3 builds the demand machinery on these foundations.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in purchase items and costs, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the second buying record. Symptom: a PARA-500-BUY beside PARA-500; stock and cost history split; planning computing from half the picture. Correction: the merge remediation per the lifecycle rules. Prevention: the one-record principle — the buying section completes on the existing record.

Error 2 — the carton rate on a unit line. Symptom: a receipt or order row whose rate belongs to a different unit than its quantity; unit costs wrong by the conversion factor; margins misstated until a review surfaces it. Correction: the document corrected through its lane; the valuation repaired per the Inventory procedures where it posted. Prevention: the pairing rule — quantity, unit, rate read together on every row — and the receiving discipline's first check.

Error 3 — the typed order rate. Symptom: Purchase Order rates recalled rather than fetched; agreed rates unapplied; matching without a reference. Correction: the buying lists completed; open orders verified. Prevention: rates on lists from sources, and the completeness read.

Error 4 — margin from the wrong cost. Symptom: selling-price reviews reading quoted rates; import margins overstated by the acquisition layer; loss-making lines reading as profitable. Correction: the reviews re-run on landed valuations. Prevention: the vocabulary rule — margin sentences use the landed valuation.

Error 5 — optimistic planning fields. Symptom: lead times entered as hopes; stock-outs by arithmetic; safety stock ratcheted after each incident instead of sized by review. Correction: fields re-entered from measured history. Prevention: the planning review on the reorder cadence, with module 8's actuals feeding it.

Error 6 — the silent cost drift. Symptom: small agreed increases accumulating unread; selling prices static while costs climb; the margin decrease nobody decided. Correction: the trend read run and the pricing hand-off executed. Prevention: the monthly trend read with written explanations and the routing rule to the selling review.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the buying section on the one record; operate purchase units with verified factors and the pairing rule; maintain buying lists with sourced rates and the two monthly reads; define the three cost figures with their sources and uses; complete the planning fields from measured reality; read the last purchase rate within its boundaries and run the trend read; and compute a landed worksheet with the comparison rule and consignment arithmetic.

Module rule 2: a cost is a defined figure with a source — one item record serving both sides, units paired with their rates, agreed rates held on lists from documents, the quoted, invoiced, and landed figures named correctly in every decision, planning fields measured not hoped, and every price movement read and routed. Module 3 covers Material Requests and the demand machinery.

material_requests.title: Procurement 3 — Material Requests: Demand Made Visible
material_requests.desc: Material Requests and the demand machinery in ZhiftERP: the field walk — type routing, need dates, justifications, and the status life; the three demand sources — manual requests, reorder auto-generation on projected quantity with the computation as justification, and order-driven demand; the screening step — stock elsewhere first, the need as stated, size and date, budget and policy — with the approval-band separation and the purchases-avoided figure; consolidation — the worksheet, the ordering arithmetic with written adjustments, the date and destination structures, the request-to-order trace, and the window discipline; transfer and issue requests with the cascade rule from branch demand to hub purchasing; and the five demand reads including the quarterly trace audit.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Material Request: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Material Request and the demand machinery in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Material Request field walk; state the four request types and what each routes to; operate the three demand sources including reorder auto-generation; run the screening step that stands between demand and commitment; consolidate requests into purchase demand with the ordering arithmetic; handle transfer and issue requests at the module boundary; and run the demand reads.

What a Material Request is. The Material Request is the demand document: a recorded statement that some part of the business needs some quantity of some item by some date. It commits nothing — no stock moves, no money is promised, no supplier is engaged. Its function is to make demand explicit, attributable, and reviewable before anything is committed, which is the structural difference between a purchasing function that responds to recorded demand and one that responds to corridor conversations.

Position in the flow. Demand precedes commitment: the Material Request sits before the Request for Quotation and the Purchase Order (modules 4-5), and before the transfer machinery on the internal side. The sequence — need recorded, need screened, need consolidated, then committed — gives the buying decision its shape: the Purchase Order commits against screened, consolidated demand, and every order line traces back to the requests that justified it.

The four types. The Material Request Type field routes the demand:

1. Purchase — the demand becomes buying: the type this track's modules 4-5 consume.
2. Material Transfer — the demand is met from another warehouse: the branch replenishment lane the Inventory track's module 6 operates.
3. Material Issue — the demand is internal consumption: stock issued to a department or purpose through the issue lane.
4. Manufacture — the demand routes to production, where the site runs the manufacturing lane.

The type is a routing decision made at the request, and Chapter 6 covers the boundary cases — including the transfer request that becomes purchase demand when the network cannot cover it.

Custody. Requests are raised by the roles the matrix permits (branch supervisors, department heads, and the reorder machinery itself); screening is the procurement function's step; approval bands per the matrix; and the standing rule: demand is recorded before it is met — no order without its requests, no request without its stated need.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: demand sources. Chapter 4: screening. Chapter 5: consolidation. Chapter 6: transfers and issues. Chapter 7: the demand reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Material Request doctype
lessons.html:
Open Material Request (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. Material Request Type. The routing decision (Chapter 1): Purchase, Material Transfer, Material Issue, or Manufacture. The type determines which machinery consumes the request and what the warehouse fields mean, so it is set first and set correctly — a transfer need typed as a purchase generates buying for stock the network already holds.

2. Requested By and the requesting context. Who raises the request, and for which part of the business — the branch, department, or cost centre per the site's fields. Attribution matters operationally: the demand reads (Chapter 7) aggregate by requester, and the screening step (Chapter 4) evaluates need in the requester's context.

3. Required By Date. The date the need becomes real — when the branch runs out, when the job starts, when the stock is needed on the shelf. The honest-date rule applies in a specific form here: the required-by date is the need date, not the wish date. Dates padded early teach the system's readers to discount them; dates entered late guarantee expediting. Every downstream schedule — the quotation cycle, the order's delivery date, the import consignment calendar — computes backward from this field.

4. The items table. Per row:

1. Item and quantity in the stated unit — the unit column read per the standing discipline; branch requests in cartons and counts in units are the module 2 pairing rule's territory.
2. The warehouse fields per type — for Purchase: the warehouse the goods should arrive into; for Material Transfer: the source and target of the movement; for Material Issue: the warehouse issuing. The fields state where the need physically is.
3. The per-row required-by date where needs differ by line.

5. The justification. The stated need — the reorder computation for auto-generated requests (Chapter 3), the branch's sales cover statement, the department's purpose for an issue. One line suffices; its presence is what the screening step reads, and a request whose need cannot be stated in a line is a request the screen returns to its raiser.

6. Save, submit, and the status life. Submission enters the request into the demand pipeline. The status tracks its life: Pending, Partially Ordered, Ordered (for purchase types — the %ordered figure per row), Transferred or Issued for the internal types, and Stopped for demand deliberately ended (Chapter 7's hygiene). A request is never deleted to make it go away; it is stopped with its reason, so the demand record stays complete.

Verification per request. The type correct for the need; the requester and context attributed; the date the need date; quantities in read units against stated warehouses; the justification present.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Demand sources
lessons.html:
Demand enters the pipeline from three sources. This chapter is each source and its rules.

1. Manual requests. Branches and departments raise requests for what they need: the branch's stock request ahead of a promotion, the department's consumables, the clinic's equipment need. The rules:

1. Raised by the permitted roles in the requester's own context — the branch requests for the branch.
2. Justified in a line (Chapter 2.5) — the sales cover, the purpose, the event.
3. Dated honestly — the need date, computed from the requester's own arithmetic (the branch that sells forty units a week and holds eighty knows its date).

2. Reorder auto-generation. The Inventory track's module 6 machinery: reorder levels on the item-warehouse rows, evaluated against projected quantity — actual stock minus reservations plus incoming orders — so the computation sees commitments in both directions. When projected quantity falls below the reorder level, the system generates a Material Request for the reorder quantity:

1. The generated request carries its computation as its justification — the level, the projected figure, the shortfall: screened like any other demand, not treated as pre-approved because a machine raised it.
2. The parameters are module 2's planning fields — measured lead times, costed safety stock, quantities in carton multiples: the auto-trigger is only as good as the fields it computes from, and the planning review is where its quality is maintained.
3. The generation runs on the configured schedule, and the reorder review (the weekly pass the Inventory track defined) reads what it generated before the screen consumes it.

3. Order-driven demand. Sales commitments generate purchase demand where stock will not cover them: the enterprise order whose equipment must be bought (the Selling track's BizRetail Ltd case triggered exactly this), the made-to-order line, the special. The rules: the demand references its driving order, its date computes backward from the order's delivery schedule with the lead time (module 2's field), and its quantities are the order's quantities — demand that borrows an order's justification to buy extra is padding the screen exists to catch.

4. The source mix as information. The demand pattern read (Chapter 7) splits the pipeline by source. The mix is operationally meaningful: a network whose demand is mostly auto-generated runs on its parameters (and its exceptions are parameter questions); one whose demand is mostly manual runs on judgment (and its exceptions are screening questions); order-driven spikes are the commercial calendar showing through. The read states the mix; the review acts on what it states.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The screening step
lessons.html:
Between recorded demand and committed money stands one procedure. This chapter is the screen.

1. What screening is. The procurement function's review of submitted requests before they consolidate into buying: each request confirmed as a genuine, correctly-sized, correctly-dated need that the network cannot meet more cheaply from what it already holds. Screening runs on the demand pipeline's cadence (daily or per the volume), and its output is requests passed, returned, or resized — each with its note.

2. The screening checks, in order.

1. Stock elsewhere first. Before any purchase: does the network hold this item idle somewhere? The Inventory track's rebalancing lane (module 7) is the first answer to demand — the lateral transfer from a branch holding dead stock costs transport; the purchase costs the full landed figure. The screen queries network stock as its first act, and a purchase request for an item another warehouse holds in excess converts to a transfer request with the note.
2. The need as stated. The justification against the requester's context: the branch's sales cover arithmetic sampled against its actual sell-through (the reads the Inventory track's module 6 built serve here); the department's purpose against its pattern. Returned requests state what was missing.
3. The size and the date. Quantity against the stated need (the pairing rule catching unit errors — a branch requesting 15 when it means 15 cartons, or the reverse); the date against the real calendar.
4. Budget and policy where configured — the request against its cost centre's frame, per the site's budget configuration; policy items (restricted classes, approval-required categories) routed to their named approvers.

3. Approval bands. Screened demand approves per the matrix: routine replenishment within the standing bands; above-band or exceptional demand to the named approvers with the screen's notes attached. The approval attaches to the demand before the money is committed — module 5's Purchase Order approval then reviews the commitment (supplier, price, terms), not the need, because the need was settled here. The two approvals ask different questions, and keeping them separate is what keeps both short.

4. The screen's record. Each screening pass files its list: requests passed with sizes confirmed, returned with reasons, converted to transfers with the stock they found. The monthly screening read (Chapter 7) samples the passes — and the specific figure it tracks is stated plainly: purchases avoided by the stock-elsewhere check, in naira, because that figure is the screen's measurable contribution and the reason the step exists.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Consolidation
lessons.html:
Screened demand consolidates into buying. This chapter is the worksheet and the arithmetic.

1. Why consolidation. The same item is demanded from several sources in the same window — the hub's reorder trigger, two branches' requests. Ordering each separately produces three small orders, three deliveries, three receipts, and none of the volume terms the supplier's price breaks offer. Consolidation combines the demand into one purchase decision per item per supplier per window, and the trace (below) keeps every source visible inside it.

2. The consolidation worksheet. Per buying window, per item:

1. The demand lines — each open, screened request row for the item: source, quantity, required-by date, destination warehouse.
2. The consolidated quantity — the sum, adjusted by the ordering arithmetic below.
3. The date structure — the earliest genuine need date governs the order's first delivery; where sources need at different dates, the consolidated order carries the schedule (module 5's per-row dates and split deliveries serve exactly this).
4. The destination structure — where the goods should land: the hub for onward distribution in the standing network pattern, or split destinations where the supplier delivers direct per the arrangement.

3. The ordering arithmetic. The consolidated quantity is shaped by module 2's constraints, applied in order: the purchase unit's multiples (orders in whole cartons), the supplier's minimums, the price-break thresholds where crossing one is priced against carrying the extra (the module 4 quotations state the breaks; the worksheet shows the comparison), and the import consignment arithmetic on foreign lines. Each adjustment above the raw demand is written on the worksheet with its reason — the excess is a decided figure, not a rounding accident.

4. The request-to-order trace. The Purchase Order (module 5) creates against the consolidated demand, and the system links each order row to its requests: %ordered advances on every source request as the order commits. The trace answers, in both directions, the two standing questions: which requests does this order serve (the order's justification), and where is my request (the requester's status view). A consolidation that loses its trace turns the demand pipeline into a suggestion box; the linkage is maintained as part of creating the order, not reconstructed afterward.

5. The window discipline. Consolidation runs on the buying calendar — the weekly window for domestic replenishment, the consignment calendar for imports — and demand arriving after a window closes waits for the next unless its date cannot wait, in which case it is the expedite lane with its named approval and its premium visible. The calendar is what makes consolidation possible; a pipeline ordered continuously in dribbles consolidates nothing.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Transfer and issue requests
lessons.html:
Two request types stay internal. This chapter is their handling and the boundary where internal demand becomes buying.

1. Material Transfer requests. The branch replenishment lane: the branch (or the reorder machinery evaluating the branch's rows) requests stock from the hub. The mechanics belong to the Inventory track's module 6 — the weekly replenishment run, the two-step transfer with the transit warehouse, the receiving confirmation — and this module's contribution is the demand side: the request raised, dated, and justified per Chapter 2, consumed by the transfer run.

2. The cascade: when transfer demand becomes purchase demand. The standing network pattern is hub-and-spoke: branches request from the hub; the hub buys from suppliers. The cascade rule:

1. The branch's request is always a transfer request — the branch's relationship is with the hub, and branch-level purchasing is the exception lane the network policy defines (the Inventory track's exception purchase lane), not a routing choice.
2. The hub's coverage check — the transfer run evaluates the hub's projected stock against the requested transfers: covered demand transfers on the run's schedule.
3. Uncovered demand cascades — the shortfall becomes purchase demand at the hub: the hub's reorder row may already have triggered (the projected figure fell as the transfer reservations landed), or the screen raises the purchase demand explicitly with the branch requests as its justification. Either way the consolidation worksheet (Chapter 5) shows the branch demand inside the purchase quantity, and the trace runs branch request → hub purchase → order.

3. Material Issue requests. Internal consumption — consumables to a department, materials to a project — requested, screened for purpose, and issued through the Inventory issue lane with the cost landing on the consuming context per the accountant's design. The issue request's discipline is the purpose statement: issues aggregate into the consumption reads, and unattributed consumption is the leak those reads exist to find.

4. The boundary, stated. This module owns demand and its screening; the Inventory track owns the movement machinery (transfers, issues, the transit discipline); modules 4-5 own the buying that uncovered demand becomes. The documents keep the boundary visible: the request states the need, the transfer or issue documents the internal movement, the order documents the commitment — one need, each stage on its own record, the trace connecting them.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The demand reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the demand pipeline, each with its cadence and action.

1. The open-demand read — weekly. All open requests by age, status, and required-by date:

1. Approaching dates — open requests whose need dates fall inside the buying lead time: each is either in a consolidation window, on an order (%ordered advancing), or a problem named now while expediting is still an option.
2. The aging tail — requests open past the policy's window with no ordering activity: each chased to its state — superseded (stopped with reason), waiting on a window (noted), or lost in the pipeline (the process finding).

2. The %ordered read — weekly, with the open-demand pass. Partially ordered requests: the unordered remainder confirmed as still needed (demand shrinks as reality changes — the remainder is re-screened, not automatically carried) or stopped. The figure per request is the requester's answer to where is my request, and keeping it true is what makes the pipeline trustworthy to its users.

3. The stale and stopped hygiene — monthly. Requests stopped in the month with their reasons aggregated; open requests with passed dates and no action swept into decisions. The pipeline's target state matches every other register in the programme: only live demand, because the consolidation worksheets and the buying calendar compute from it.

4. The demand pattern read — monthly. The pipeline by source (Chapter 3.4), requester, and item class:

1. The source mix and its movement — auto-generation's share rising as parameters mature is the intended direction; manual spikes trace to their events.
2. The requester patterns — branches whose requests consistently resize at screening (over-asking as negotiation) are a conversation with data; branches that never request until stock-out are the opposite conversation.
3. The screening figures — returned and converted requests by reason, and the purchases-avoided figure (Chapter 4.4) stated in naira.

5. The trace audit — quarterly. A sample of the quarter's Purchase Orders walked backward: each order row to its requests, each request to its justification. The audit confirms the standing rule holds — no order without its demand — and its findings are process corrections: the order raised without requests (the corridor purchase the pipeline exists to end), the trace lost at consolidation, the justification that was a formality. The audit files with the procurement function's quarterly records, alongside the module 8 scorecard cycle.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the 300-carton consolidation
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the demand machinery through the standing case: the PARA-500 purchase that module 5 will place with Emzor. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the auto-trigger (Chapter 3). The weekly reorder evaluation at Central Warehouse computes PARA-500's projected quantity — actual stock minus the sales reservations, plus nothing incoming — below the reorder level. The machinery generates a Material Request, type Purchase, for 260 cartons, carrying its computation as the justification: the level, the projected figure, the shortfall, the reorder quantity in carton multiples per the planning fields.

Step 2 — the branch requests (Chapters 3, 6). The same week, two branches raise transfer requests for PARA-500 ahead of their local demand: Ibadan for 15 cartons, Akure for 25 cartons — each justified with its sales cover arithmetic, each dated to its need. The transfer run's coverage check finds the hub's projected stock — already below reorder — cannot cover the transfers: the branch demand cascades into the hub's purchase demand per the cascade rule, the branch requests standing as part of its justification.

Step 3 — the screen (Chapter 4). The screening pass works the three demands: the stock-elsewhere check runs first and finds no idle PARA-500 anywhere in the network (the rebalancing lane has nothing to offer — this is genuine new demand); the branch arithmetic samples clean against sell-through; the units read correctly (cartons throughout, per the pairing rule); the dates hold. All three pass, with the screen's notes filed.

Step 4 — the consolidation worksheet (Chapter 5). The buying window consolidates PARA-500: 260 (Central reorder) + 15 (Ibadan) + 25 (Akure) = 300 cartons. The ordering arithmetic confirms the figure: whole cartons already; above Emzor's minimum; the quantity sits at the volume band the standing arrangement prices (module 4's cycle established the rates — the order will place at ₦9,600 per carton). The date structure records the earliest genuine need — Central's cover date — and notes that the branches' dates allow the second drop: the worksheet anticipates the two-drop schedule module 5 will commit (180 next week, 120 the week after), driven by the dates the requests stated.

Step 5 — the trace stands (Chapters 5, 7). Module 5's Purchase Order will create against this consolidated demand, and at that moment %ordered advances on all three requests: the Central trigger, Ibadan's 15, Akure's 25 — each requester's status view answering where their request went. The quarter's trace audit will walk this order backward and find the complete chain: order → worksheet → three requests → three justifications — the standing rule holding: no order without its demand.

The pipeline evidence. The requests with their justifications; the screen's pass with the stock-elsewhere check recorded; the worksheet with the arithmetic and the date structure; the trace ready for the order. Module 4 covers how the Emzor rates on this worksheet were established; module 5 places the commitment.
