lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in demand management, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the corridor purchase. Symptom: Purchase Orders raised from conversations with no requests behind them; demand invisible, unattributable, unscreened. Correction: the demand recorded retroactively where the purchase was genuine; the trace audit's finding filed. Prevention: the standing rule enforced in configuration where the site gates orders on requests, and the quarterly trace audit.

Error 2 — the wish date. Symptom: required-by dates padded early as negotiation or entered late as afterthought; downstream schedules computing from fiction; readers discounting all dates. Correction: dates corrected to need dates at screening. Prevention: the need-date rule and the screening date check.

Error 3 — the purchase for stock the network holds. Symptom: buying while another warehouse holds the item in excess; dead stock accumulating at one site while money is spent at another. Correction: the request converted to a transfer; the purchase avoided. Prevention: the stock-elsewhere check as the screen's first act, with its avoided-purchases figure read monthly.

Error 4 — auto-generation treated as pre-approved. Symptom: machine-generated requests ordered without screening; parameter errors (a stale reorder level, an optimistic lead time) buying at scale. Correction: the parameters reviewed; the excess handled through the stock-health lanes. Prevention: generated requests screened like any other, and the planning review maintaining the fields.

Error 5 — the lost trace. Symptom: orders that cannot name their requests; requesters who cannot find their demand; %ordered figures meaning nothing. Correction: the linkage rebuilt for open documents. Prevention: the trace maintained as part of order creation, and the quarterly audit.

Error 6 — the immortal request. Symptom: open requests aging past their dates and their needs; the pipeline cluttered with dead demand; consolidation worksheets summing fiction. Correction: the aging tail swept — stopped with reasons or re-dated as re-screened demand. Prevention: the weekly open-demand read and the monthly hygiene.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the request walk with the type routing, need dates, and justifications; operate the three demand sources including the auto-trigger's computation; run the four screening checks in order with the approval-band separation; consolidate with the worksheet, the ordering arithmetic, and the window discipline; handle the transfer cascade and the issue lane at the boundary; and run the five demand reads.

Module rule 3: demand is recorded before it is met — typed correctly, dated to the need, justified in a line, screened with stock-elsewhere first, consolidated by the worksheet's written arithmetic, and traced so that every order names its requests and every requester can find their demand. Module 4 covers Requests for Quotation and the comparison cycle.

rfq_quotes.title: Procurement 4 — RFQs & Supplier Quotations: The Sourcing Craft
rfq_quotes.desc: Requests for Quotation and the comparison cycle in ZhiftERP: when the policy requires competitive quotes and the named recorded exceptions; the Request for Quotation walk — supplier selection, consolidated quantities, the complete message, and the managed response window; Supplier Quotation entry from attached documents with the pairing rule, tiered breaks, and foreign-currency handling; the comparison worksheet with the landed centre column and the stated criteria; the award decision — best total position, split awards, the decision minute with alternatives, and the updates to lists, orders, and supplier files; negotiation from the recorded position, volume bands, standing arrangements with real validity, and the owned re-quote calendar; and the five cycle reads including the quarterly savings record.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The quotation cycle: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers Requests for Quotation, Supplier Quotations, and the comparison cycle in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: state when the policy requires competitive quotation; complete the Request for Quotation walk and issue it to suppliers; enter Supplier Quotations from source documents; build the comparison worksheet with landed figures; run the award decision with its criteria and record; conduct the negotiation round and establish standing arrangements; and run the cycle reads.

What the cycle is. The quotation cycle converts screened demand into priced supply options and a recorded award decision: the business asks named suppliers what they would charge, records what each answered, compares the answers on stated criteria, and decides — with the decision, its reasoning, and its alternatives filed. The cycle's product is not only a price: it is the negotiation memory module 2's buying lists draw their sourced rates from, and the record every later price conversation is conducted against.

When the cycle is required. Per the written procurement policy:

1. By value — purchases above the policy's threshold require competitive quotes (the number of quotes per band stated in the policy).
2. By class — the classes the policy names (new items, capital equipment, annual arrangements) quote regardless of single-purchase value, because the arrangement's total exposure is the relevant figure.
3. The exceptions, named — single-source items (the sole manufacturer of a registered product), genuine emergencies through the expedite lane, and repeat purchases inside a standing arrangement's validity — each exception recorded with its reason, because an unrecorded exception is indistinguishable from an avoided control.

Position in the flow. Demand (module 3) precedes the cycle; the cycle's award feeds the Purchase Order (module 5) and the buying lists (module 2); the supplier's later performance (module 8's scorecards) feeds the next cycle's comparison. The sequence gives procurement its accountability shape: every rate on an order traces to a quotation or arrangement, and every award can state why it was made.

Custody. The procurement function runs the cycle; award decisions approve per the matrix's bands; the comparison and decision records file per the one-lookup standard; and the standing rule: a quoted rate is evidence — entered from the supplier's document, compared landed, awarded by stated criteria, and filed with its alternatives.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Request for Quotation. Chapter 3: Supplier Quotation entry. Chapter 4: the comparison worksheet. Chapter 5: the award decision. Chapter 6: negotiation and arrangements. Chapter 7: the cycle reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Request for Quotation
lessons.html:
Open Request for Quotation (awesome bar) > New. Complete the fields in order.

1. The suppliers table. The named suppliers the request goes to — selected from the register (module 1's gate is the entry point; the cycle does not quote unregistered parties), per the policy's count for the band, drawn from the classes the item belongs to. Supplier selection is itself recorded reasoning: the incumbents, the qualified alternatives, and — where the read shows the same short list every cycle — the deliberate widening the competitiveness review directs.

2. The items table. Drawn from the driving Material Requests (the link carries the demand trace through the cycle):

1. Item, quantity, and unit — the consolidated quantities from module 3's worksheet, in the purchase units, because rates will be quoted against these quantities and volume terms depend on them.
2. Required-by schedule — the dates the demand stated: suppliers quote lead times against real dates.
3. Warehouse — the delivery destination, because delivered-to-where is part of what is being priced (the supplier's included delivery versus ex-works collection changes the landed comparison).

3. The message to suppliers. The request's terms: the response deadline, the validity period expected on quotes, the requirement to state price breaks, minimums, lead times, and payment terms, and the specification references for items that carry them. A request that does not ask for breaks and terms receives quotes that omit them, and the comparison then runs on incomplete columns — the request's completeness determines the comparison's.

4. Issuing the request. The request sends per the site's channels — the emailed document, or the supplier portal link where the site operates portal quoting (suppliers entering their own rates against the request, which lands the responses as draft Supplier Quotations directly). Either channel, the same record rule: what was asked, of whom, by when, filed on the request.

5. The response window. The deadline is managed, not hoped: the reminder at the mid-point to non-responders, the response log as quotes arrive, and the close at the deadline — late quotes admitted only by the recorded exception (the policy states when), because a comparison whose window silently extends for one supplier is not the level comparison the file claims. Non-response is itself data: the response-rate read (Chapter 7) accumulates it per supplier, and module 8's relationship review consumes it.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Supplier Quotation entry
lessons.html:
Each response is recorded as a Supplier Quotation. This chapter is the entry discipline.

1. The Supplier Quotation doctype. Open Supplier Quotation (awesome bar) — or receive it from the portal as a draft. The record per responding supplier:

1. The supplier and the request reference — the link to the Request for Quotation carrying the cycle's thread.
2. The items table — the quoted rate per item per unit, the quoted lead time, and the quantity terms.
3. Validity — the date the quote holds until: the field the award clock runs against, and the field the re-quote cadence (Chapter 6) watches.
4. Terms — payment terms offered, delivery terms (included delivery or ex-works — the landed comparison's input), and any conditions the supplier attaches.

2. The entry discipline. Quotes entered by the procurement function follow the evidence rule:

1. From the supplier's document — the emailed quotation, the price circular, the signed offer — attached to the Supplier Quotation. The record states what the supplier stated; the attachment proves it. A rate entered from a phone call is entered with the call noted and confirmed in writing before the comparison closes, because an award justified by an unverifiable rate is an award that cannot defend itself.
2. The pairing rule at entry — the quoted rate belongs to a quoted unit: ₦9,600 per Carton-12 entered as such, never transcribed onto a unit line. Transcription is where comparison errors are born, and the entry check reads quantity-unit-rate together per the standing discipline.
3. Breaks entered as breaks — a supplier quoting tiered rates (one rate to 199 cartons, a better rate from 200, better again from 300) has each tier recorded, because the comparison at the consolidated quantity needs the tier that quantity lands in, and the consolidation arithmetic (module 3) may deliberately cross a tier.

3. Foreign-currency quotes. The Indian manufacturer quotes in dollars: the Supplier Quotation carries the quoted currency and rate as quoted, and the comparison worksheet (Chapter 4) does the conversion at the planning rate — the quote records the supplier's statement; the worksheet does the arithmetic. Converting at entry buries the exposure the comparison must show.

4. Clarifications. Ambiguities — a quote silent on delivery terms, a break structure unclear — are resolved by written question and answer filed with the quotation, before comparison. A comparison built on assumed readings of ambiguous quotes produces awards the supplier will dispute at the first invoice.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The comparison worksheet
lessons.html:
Recorded quotes compare on one worksheet. This chapter is its columns and its rules.

1. The worksheet's shape. Per item (or per lot where items award together): one row per quoting supplier, columns per criterion, the consolidated quantity from module 3 as the comparison quantity, and the file reference per row to the Supplier Quotation it summarises. The worksheet is a record, not a scratchpad: it files with the decision, and the trace audit expects to find it.

2. The landed column — the comparison's centre. Per module 2's comparison rule, suppliers compare landed, never ex-works:

1. Domestic quotes with included delivery — the quoted rate is close to the landed figure; the worksheet notes any excluded charges.
2. Ex-works and foreign quotes — the landed worksheet (module 2, Chapter 7) computes the full figure: goods value converted at the planning rate, plus freight, insurance, duties, clearing, and haulage. The Indian manufacturer's attractive dollar rate is compared only after it becomes a naira-per-unit-on-the-shelf figure.
3. The rule in one sentence: the comparison column is what the item will cost on the shelf, from each supplier, at the comparison quantity — anything else compares fragments.

3. The other columns. Price is one criterion:

1. Lead time — quoted, and adjusted by the supplier's measured reality where module 8's data exists (a quoted two weeks from a supplier whose measured performance is four is entered as quoted with the measured figure beside it).
2. Payment terms — the working-capital value of offered terms, computed per the accountant's arithmetic where terms differ materially.
3. Quality and performance — the scorecard figures (module 8) for known suppliers: on-time rate, damage rate, dispute history. New suppliers carry their verification status and any trial-order condition.
4. Minimums, breaks, and validity — stated per quote, with the break tier at the comparison quantity marked.

4. The total-cost view. Where criteria pull in different directions, the worksheet computes the comparable total: the landed rate at the comparison quantity, adjusted for the terms value, with the risk criteria (lead time, performance) stated beside the money rather than converted into it by invented weights. The decision (Chapter 5) weighs the stated figures; the worksheet's job is to state them honestly and completely, one page per item, readable by an approver who was not in the cycle.

The column people forget to build. Lead time against the demand's required-by date. A worksheet comparing landed money alone will award to a supplier whose delivery lands after the stock-out the purchase was raised to prevent — which is a saving of a few percent bought with an empty shelf. Put the date beside the money and the comparison answers the question the demand actually asked.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The award decision
lessons.html:
The comparison feeds a decision. This chapter is the criteria, the record, and what the award updates.

1. The decision criteria. Per the written policy, the award goes to the best total position, not reflexively to the lowest rate:

1. The landed figure at the real quantity — the money criterion, from the worksheet's centre column.
2. Supply reliability — the measured performance and lead time against the demand's dates: the lowest rate that arrives late costs its saving in stock-outs, and the policy states how reliability is weighed for the class (essential lines weigh it heavily; discretionary lines less).
3. Terms and relationship structure — the payment terms' value, the arrangement potential (Chapter 6), and the concentration position (module 1's read: an award that deepens a named dependency is made knowingly or not at all).

2. Split awards. The decision may split: the volume line to the best landed position, a secondary share to the qualified alternative — the deliberate dual-sourcing the concentration review recommends on critical classes, priced as the policy allows (the secondary share may carry a premium, stated in the minute as the cost of supply security). A split is a decision with its reasoning, not an inability to decide.

3. The decision minute. One page, filed with the worksheet:

1. The award: supplier(s), items, rates, quantities or bands, terms, validity.
2. The reasoning: the criteria as weighed for this decision, in two or three sentences.
3. The alternatives: what the unsuccessful quotes offered, in one line each — the record that makes next cycle's negotiation informed and this cycle's decision defensible.
4. The approval: per the matrix's band for the award's value.

4. What the award updates.

1. The buying lists — the awarded rates load by the governed update with the minute as their source: module 2's sourced-rates rule closing its loop.
2. The demand pipeline — module 5's Purchase Order creates against the screened demand at the awarded rates; the trace runs request → worksheet → award → order.
3. The supplier file — the award, and equally the non-award, files per supplier: module 8's relationship review reads both.

5. Unsuccessful suppliers. Informed per the policy's courtesy standard — the relationship the business may need next cycle is maintained by the professionalism of this one. The notification's content follows the policy (the fact of the award; commercial details per the confidentiality rules), and the response-rate read expects continued participation as its measure of whether the cycle treats its participants well.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Negotiation and standing arrangements
lessons.html:
The comparison creates a negotiating position; repeat lines convert awards into arrangements. This chapter is both.

1. The negotiation round. Between comparison and award, the policy permits a negotiation round with the leading suppliers:

1. Conducted from the worksheet — the position is the recorded alternatives; the asks are specific (the rate at the volume tier, the terms, the included delivery) and minuted as asked and answered.
2. The level-field rule — the round's structure follows the policy (best-and-final from the shortlist, or sequential negotiation as the policy allows); one supplier's quote is not disclosed to another, because a cycle that leaks quotes teaches suppliers to quote high and wait.
3. The outcome enters the record — negotiated improvements amend the Supplier Quotation (the supplier's confirming document attached) and the worksheet re-states before the award minute writes.

2. Volume bands. The negotiation's standing instrument for repeat lines: the rate agreed per quantity band — the tier structure entered from Chapter 3 becoming the agreed schedule. The consolidated ordering (module 3) then prices predictably: the 300-carton window lands in its band at its rate, and the ordering arithmetic can deliberately reach a band where the worksheet shows the crossing pays.

3. Standing arrangements. For lines bought repeatedly, the award converts into an arrangement — the agreed rates (or bands), terms, and validity period, recorded per the site's instrument (the supplier-specific price structure, or the buying-side blanket order where quantities commit):

1. Inside validity, purchases execute without re-quoting — the module 1 exception operating as designed: the cycle ran once at the arrangement's scale.
2. The validity is real — expiry triggers the re-quote cadence (below); rates do not drift past their period by inattention, per the same rule as the selling side's blanket orders.
3. Price-change requests inside validity — the supplier's increase letter routes to the review: accepted changes are dated amendments with the notice filed; the trend read (module 2) shows what moved and when.

4. The re-quote cadence. Per class in the policy: annual for stable domestic lines, semi-annual where markets move, per-consignment elements on import lines (freight re-quotes with the market even where goods rates hold). The cadence is calendared with the quarterly cycle reads, so re-quoting is scheduled work rather than a response to a supplier's letter — the business that only re-quotes when a supplier raises prices has ceded the calendar to its suppliers.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The cycle reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the quotation cycle, each with its cadence and action.

1. The open-cycle read — weekly. Open Requests for Quotation by response deadline and age: reminders to non-responders at the midpoint; cycles past deadline closed and compared; cycles stalled before award chased to their blocking step — a demand pipeline waiting on a stalled cycle is a stock-out forming upstream, and the read connects the two dates.

2. The validity read — weekly. Supplier Quotations and arrangements by days-to-expiry: awards pending against expiring quotes decided before the clock runs out (an award made against an expired quote is a re-quote conducted involuntarily); arrangements approaching expiry entering the re-quote calendar per Chapter 6.

3. The response-rate read — quarterly. Per supplier: requests sent, responses received, response timeliness. The patterns route: the reliable responder is the relationship working; the chronic non-responder is a module 8 conversation (and, unresolved, a register question — a supplier that will not quote is a supplier in name); a class where response rates fall across suppliers is a market signal the review reads.

4. The award pattern read — quarterly. The quarter's awards by supplier, class, and value:

1. The competitiveness figure — cycles with the policy's quote count achieved, against cycles that ran short (with reasons: genuine single-source, or a supplier base too thin — the widening action).
2. The concentration movement — awards' effect on the module 1 concentration figures, read together with the risk review.
3. The incumbency pattern — the incumbent's win rate: a rate near one hundred percent with prices drifting upward is the signal that the cycle has become a formality, and the deliberate-widening action (new qualified suppliers into the next cycle) is its correction.

5. The savings record — quarterly. The cycle's measured contribution: negotiated improvements against first quotes, band crossings that paid, and the avoided-cost figures where re-quoting moved an incumbent's drift back — stated in naira with the cycles referenced, filed with the procurement function's quarterly records alongside module 3's purchases-avoided figure. The two figures together are the demand-and-sourcing machinery's stated value, in money, per quarter — the record the owner's review reads when the function's cost is weighed against its contribution.

The read that costs nothing and changes the base. How often does the same short list appear? A cycle that goes to the same three suppliers every time is not competitive procurement, however correctly each cycle is run — it is a habit with paperwork. The competitiveness review exists to name that pattern and direct a deliberate widening, and it is the only mechanism in the module that acts on the supply base rather than on individual purchases.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: establishing the Emzor arrangement
lessons.html:
This chapter runs the cycle that produced the ₦9,600 rate the module 3 consolidation priced from. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

The trigger. PARA-500's volume and the class policy (annual arrangements for core pharmaceutical lines) put the line into the annual quotation cycle: the consolidated annual volume justifies arrangement-scale negotiation rather than order-by-order pricing.

Step 1 — the request issues (Chapter 2). The Request for Quotation goes to three registered suppliers: Emzor, the second domestic manufacturer, and the importer channel as the qualified alternative. The items table carries the annual volume structure and the delivery destination (Central Warehouse); the message asks for price breaks by quantity band, payment terms, lead times, and validity; the deadline is set with the mid-point reminder calendared.

Step 2 — the quotations enter (Chapter 3). All three respond. Each Supplier Quotation enters from the supplier's attached document, rates paired to units (per Carton-12 throughout), break structures recorded as tiers — including Emzor's tiering with its band at the 300-carton volume level. The importer's quote notes ex-works terms; the clarification round confirms it in writing.

Step 3 — the comparison (Chapter 4). The worksheet compares landed at the annual and per-window quantities: the domestic manufacturers' included-delivery rates stand nearly as quoted; the importer's rate gains the acquisition layer and loses its apparent advantage — the landed column re-ordering the ranking the raw rates suggested. The other columns fill: lead times (with measured history beside Emzor's quote), terms offered, and the scorecard figures for the incumbents.

Step 4 — negotiation and award (Chapters 5-6). The negotiation round runs from the worksheet with the two domestic manufacturers: the specific asks — the band rate and terms — minuted as asked and answered. The award decision: Emzor takes the volume line at ₦9,600 per Carton-12 at the volume band, on 30-day terms, with the second manufacturer holding a secondary share on the overlap range — the split stated in the minute as the concentration mitigation the module 1 risk review recommended, with its premium visible. The decision minute files with the worksheet: award, reasoning in three sentences, alternatives in a line each, approval per the band.

Step 5 — the award updates the machinery (Chapters 5-6). The rates load onto the buying list by the governed update, the minute as source; the arrangement records with its validity and the re-quote date calendared; the unsuccessful importer is informed per the courtesy standard and remains a responsive participant in the read. When module 3's consolidation later sums 300 cartons, the worksheet prices from this arrangement without re-quoting — the band rate applying exactly as agreed — and module 5's order will commit it.

The cycle evidence. The request with its message; three quotations with attached documents; the worksheet with its landed centre; the negotiation minutes; the decision minute with alternatives; the sourced rate on the list; the calendar entry for re-quote. The rate every PARA-500 order carries is answerable back to this file in one lookup — the negotiation memory the module exists to build.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in the quotation cycle, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the ex-works comparison. Symptom: rankings built on raw quoted rates; the import line awarded on a figure that omits its acquisition layer; the shelf cost discovered after commitment. Correction: the worksheet rebuilt landed; the award reviewed. Prevention: the landed column as the comparison's centre, per the module 2 rule.

Error 2 — the unverifiable rate. Symptom: quotes entered from calls with no confirming document; awards that cannot show what the supplier actually offered; disputes at the first invoice. Correction: written confirmation obtained or the quote excluded. Prevention: entry from attached documents, and phone rates confirmed in writing before comparison closes.

Error 3 — the leaked cycle. Symptom: one supplier's rates disclosed to another; suppliers learning to quote high and wait for the leak; the comparison's integrity gone. Correction: the round's records reviewed; the policy's structure re-imposed. Prevention: the level-field rule, and negotiation conducted from the worksheet's recorded position rather than from disclosures.

Error 4 — the formality cycle. Symptom: the incumbent winning every cycle at drifting prices; requests issued to the same short list; the comparison a ritual before a foregone award. Correction: the deliberate widening — new qualified suppliers into the next cycle. Prevention: the award pattern read's incumbency figure, acted on.

Error 5 — the undocumented award. Symptom: rates on orders with no minute behind them; decisions that cannot state their criteria; the next negotiation starting from nothing. Correction: the record reconstructed where evidence allows. Prevention: the decision minute as the award's required form, and the trace audit expecting it.

Error 6 — the expired arrangement still pricing. Symptom: purchases at arrangement rates past validity; increases accepted without dated amendments; the calendar ceded to supplier letters. Correction: the re-quote run; rates re-established. Prevention: the validity read and the calendared re-quote cadence per class.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state when the policy requires the cycle and the recorded exceptions; issue a complete request with breaks, terms, and deadlines asked; enter quotations from documents with the pairing rule and tiers; build the worksheet with the landed centre and the stated criteria; run the award with its minute, splits, and updates; conduct the negotiation round and maintain arrangements with real validity; and run the five cycle reads with the savings record.

Module rule 4: a quoted rate is evidence — asked completely, entered from the supplier's document, compared landed at the real quantity, awarded by stated criteria in a filed minute with its alternatives, loaded to the lists with its source, and re-quoted on the calendar the business owns. Module 5 covers the Purchase Order.

purchase_orders.title: Procurement 5 — Purchase Orders: The Commitment
purchase_orders.desc: The Purchase Order in ZhiftERP: the field walk — the demand trace, sourced rates, per-row Required By dates, warehouses, and the supplier confirmation; submission effects — incoming quantities raising projected stock and standing the trigger down, the %received and %billed execution basis, and what submission does not do; multi-drop schedules with split rows, the band-across-the-order rule, the incoming planning read, and the chase ladder; the amendment taxonomy — rate changes under award governance, quantity increases through the screen, schedule movements with parties, and the Closed status; the purchase tax side, withholding located at payment, and supplier advances with the exposure read; and the order book's six reads including stale-order hygiene as stock-out prevention.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Order: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Purchase Order in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Purchase Order field walk with the demand trace and the sourced rates; state what submission commits and what it updates; structure multi-drop delivery schedules; operate the amendment and cancellation discipline; configure the purchase tax side and handle supplier advances; and run the order book reads.

What a Purchase Order is. The Purchase Order is the buying commitment: the business commits to buy these items, in these quantities, at these rates, delivered on this schedule, on these terms. Everything before it prepared the decision — the demand recorded and screened (module 3), the rates established (module 4); everything after it executes: the receipts arrive against it (module 6), the invoices match against it (module 7), and the supplier's performance measures against it (module 8). The order is the document both parties are held to, and its correctness at submission is what makes every downstream control a comparison rather than an investigation.

Order sources.

1. From consolidated demand — the standing path: the order creates against module 3's worksheet, drawing the Material Requests so the trace links automatically and %ordered advances on every source request.
2. From an arrangement — repeat lines inside a standing arrangement's validity: the demand still traces; the rates draw from the arrangement without a new cycle (module 4's exception operating as designed).
3. The expedite lane — the genuine emergency, with its named approval and its premium visible, per module 3's window discipline.

What submission does, stated in advance. Chapter 3 details it: the ordered quantities enter the incoming figures the stock system carries (projected quantity rises), the receiving and matching machinery gains its basis, and the supplier is engaged on a document. An unsubmitted draft engages nobody; a submitted order commits the business's money and the supplier's capacity.

Custody. The procurement function prepares orders; approval per the matrix's bands reviews the commitment — supplier, rate, terms, schedule — the need having been settled at the screen (module 3's separation); rate changes after submission re-enter the award governance; and the standing rule: the order states the whole purchase — its demand, its rates' sources, its schedule, and its terms — and nothing about the purchase changes without its documented amendment.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: submission effects. Chapter 4: the delivery schedule. Chapter 5: amendments and cancellations. Chapter 6: taxes and the money side. Chapter 7: the order book reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Purchase Order doctype
lessons.html:
Create the Purchase Order from its source — the Material Requests or the consolidation view — so the trace carries. Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Supplier and the header pre-fill. The supplier selection pulls module 1's chain: the billing currency, the payment terms template, the addresses and contact. The header is read before the rows — an order in the wrong currency is wrong on every figure.

2. The items table. Per row:

1. Item, quantity, unit — from the consolidated demand, in the purchase units, the pairing rule read on every row (the quantity-unit-rate check from module 2 applies at order preparation as its first natural checkpoint).
2. Rate — from the buying list or arrangement, carrying its source (module 4's award); a rate differing from the sourced figure is a question answered before submission, not a field adjusted to proceed.
3. Required By (per row) — the schedule field: each row carries its delivery date, which is how one order states a multi-drop schedule (Chapter 4). The dates come from the demand's date structure on the worksheet.
4. Warehouse (per row) — where each row's goods should arrive: the hub in the standing pattern; split destinations where the arrangement delivers direct.
5. The Material Request links — carried by creation from the source: the trace that advances %ordered and answers the audit.

3. Taxes and Charges. The purchase taxes template per the context (Chapter 6): VAT as the supplier will charge it, so the order's total states the commitment as it will be invoiced.

4. Terms and references. The payment terms template from the supplier record (the negotiated 30 days computing the eventual invoice's due date); the arrangement or quotation reference; the supplier's own reference where one exists.

5. Save, review, submit. Draft review per the value band — the approver reviews the commitment: the supplier against the award, the rates against their sources, the schedule against the demand's dates, the total against the band. Submission commits (Chapter 3) and the order transmits to the supplier's sales contact (module 1's named person) per the site's channel, with the transmission recorded.

6. The supplier's confirmation. The order asks for confirmation: the supplier's acknowledgment of quantities, rates, and — critically — the delivery dates. The confirmation (or the silence the chase read surfaces) files on the order. An unconfirmed schedule is a hope; the confirmation converts it into the supplier's stated commitment, which is what module 8's on-time measurement runs against.

Verification per order. Header currency and terms; rows paired and sourced; per-row dates from the demand; warehouses stated; taxes per template; the trace present; then submit, transmit, and obtain confirmation.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Submission effects
lessons.html:
Submission converts the draft into a commitment. This chapter states each effect and its consequence.

1. The incoming figures. Each submitted row's undelivered quantity enters the item-warehouse's ordered quantity: projected quantity — actual minus reserved plus incoming — rises by the order. The consequences:

1. The reorder machinery sees the pipeline — the auto-trigger (module 3) computes on projected quantity, so a submitted order stops the same shortfall re-triggering: the engine does not order twice for one gap, provided orders submit promptly. A consolidation decided but not committed leaves the trigger armed — one of the reasons the buying window closes with orders submitted, not with worksheets approved.
2. Availability answers include the pipeline — the selling side's scheduling against stock (the Selling track, module 4) reads projected figures that now include this order and its dates.

2. The execution basis. The submitted order becomes the reference the downstream documents draw from:

1. Purchase Receipts create against the order (module 6): quantities receive against ordered rows, and %received tracks fulfilment per row.
2. Purchase Invoices match against the order and its receipts (module 7): %billed tracks the claim, and the three-way comparison — ordered, received, billed — is the matching control's shape.
3. The two percentages state the order's life; the gaps between them are Chapter 7's reads.

3. The supplier's commercial position. The transmitted order binds both parties on its terms: the rates and quantities per the award, the schedule per the rows, the terms per the template. From confirmation, schedule movements are events with owners — the supplier's delay is a chase-ladder entry and a scorecard fact (module 8); the business's own change is an amendment (Chapter 5).

4. What submission does not do. It moves no stock (receipts do), creates no liability (invoices do), and pays nothing (payment entries do, on the invoice's due date). The order is the commitment; the downstream documents are the performance — the same promise-versus-performance separation as the selling side, and the reason the matching control in module 7 has three distinct documents to compare.

5. The commitment value. The order book's total (Chapter 7) is money the business has committed but not yet spent: the owner's forward view of purchasing reads it weekly, and the cash planning (the payables due profile from module 1's summary) extends it — committed orders become invoices become due dates, and the three views read together are the buying side's cash forecast.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The delivery schedule
lessons.html:
Real purchases arrive in drops. This chapter is the scheduling machinery on the buying side.

1. Per-row schedule dates. The items table carries Required By per row — the mechanism for every schedule shape:

1. The single-drop order — all rows on one date.
2. The multi-drop order — the same item split across rows with different dates: the 300-carton purchase entered as two rows — 180 on the first date, 120 on the second — each row receiving independently, %received advancing per drop. The split-row structure is the standing method because each drop is then its own schedule commitment, chased and measured on its own date.
3. The rule: the rows state the schedule the demand's dates require and the supplier confirmed — the same real-plan rule as the selling side, because every planning read below computes from these dates.

2. Why multi-drop. The structure serves both parties and is priced knowingly:

1. The business's side — stock arrives as the cover dates require rather than all at once: warehouse capacity, shelf-life freshness on dated goods (later drops manufactured later), and cash timing (invoicing commonly follows delivery, so drops spread the payable).
2. The supplier's side — production and logistics scheduling against confirmed dates.
3. The volume term holds across the order — the arrangement's band prices the order's total quantity, not each drop: 300 cartons at the band rate, delivered 180 and 120, is one commercial commitment on one order — which is what makes the multi-drop structure superior to two separate orders that would each miss the band.

3. The incoming planning read — weekly. Open order rows by required-by date:

1. The coming window — rows due in the horizon, grouped by warehouse: the receiving workload (module 6's dock plans from it) and the stock arrivals the selling side's availability reads.
2. The overdue rows — rows past date and unreceived: each chased per the ladder below.
3. The at-risk rows — confirmed dates the supplier has signalled against, or unconfirmed rows inside their lead time: flagged while alternatives (the split to the secondary supplier, the expedite) are still open.

4. The chase ladder. Overdue incoming runs a stepped procedure, mirroring the collections gears in structure: the query at the date (the row is due — where is it), the escalation at the interval (the supplier's named contact, then the relationship level), and the sourcing decision where the delay breaks the cover (the secondary supplier's share activating per the split award, the expedite lane, or the customer-side conversation where a sales commitment depends on it). Every step records on the order — the delay's history is module 8's on-time evidence, per drop, per date.

5. Schedule changes. Date movements are amendments (Chapter 5) with their party recorded: the supplier's slip is their event (chased and scored); the business's deferral is its own (communicated and documented). The schedule's history then states what was committed, what moved, whose movement it was — the record the module 8 review and any commercial dispute reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Amendments and cancellations
lessons.html:
Commitments change; the record must change correctly. This chapter is the buying-side discipline.

1. The change taxonomy. Changes route by what they touch:

1. Rate changes — a rate on a submitted order moves only within the award's governance: the arrangement's dated amendment (module 4, Chapter 6), or a re-award for material changes. A supplier's request to invoice above the order's rate is a matching exception (module 7), not an order edit to make the mismatch disappear — the order states the agreed rate precisely so the invoice can be compared to it.
2. Quantity changes — increases are new demand: screened (module 3) and approved per the band, because an order amendment is not a route around the screen. Decreases release incoming (projected quantity falls — the reorder engine may re-trigger, correctly) and are checked against the supplier's position per the arrangement's terms (a band-priced order reduced below its band is a rate conversation, stated before the amendment, not discovered at the invoice).
3. Schedule changes — per Chapter 4.5: the movement, its party, its reason, the confirmation updated.
4. Administrative changes — references and contacts: ordinary edits with notes.

2. The amendment mechanics. The controlled lanes:

1. The update facility for submitted orders — quantity and schedule updates on unreceived rows, role-limited, system-logged: the standard lane.
2. Cancel-and-amend — structural changes: the order cancels with reason and the amended version carries the reference; receipts already posted gate what cancellation is possible, and an order with received drops amends around its performed portion.
3. Either lane: the change, the reason, the approver per the taxonomy, the supplier's agreement where the commercial position moved — on the document trail.

3. Cancellations. The order that will not proceed cancels with its reason code (demand ceased, supplier failure, superseded by re-award), releasing its incoming figures and closing its schedule rows. The supplier is informed formally — a cancelled order the supplier still manufactures against is a dispute in preparation — and the cancellation's cause files where it belongs: supplier-failure cancellations are scorecard facts; demand-ceased cancellations route back to module 3's pipeline hygiene.

4. The Closed status. The deliberate early end: the remainder will not be taken, incoming releases, the record preserves what happened — used at the stale-order read (Chapter 7) with its reason, per the same rule as every early closure in the programme.

5. The amendments read — monthly. Orders amended in the month: the change, the lane, the approver, reconciled against the taxonomy — rate changes carrying award governance, quantity increases carrying screens, schedule changes carrying parties and confirmations. The buying side's fields-move-by-decision audit, filed with the month's records.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Taxes and the money side
lessons.html:
The order carries the purchase's tax structure and, where terms require, its advance. This chapter is the money side before the invoice.

1. Purchase Taxes and Charges. The buying mirror of the selling template: ordered rows, each a charge with its type, account head, and rate — maintained by the accountant, selected on documents:

1. The VAT row — the supplier's VAT as it will be charged: on standard-rated purchases, 7.5% on the net, with the account head per the accountant's input-VAT design. The order's total then states the commitment as the invoice will state the claim, and the matching comparison (module 7) includes the tax arithmetic.
2. Item-level treatments — exempt purchases (the pharmaceutical classes on the buying side) compute per line through the item tax templates, exactly as the selling side: one document, mixed treatments, no hand edits.
3. The recoverability question is the accountant's — input VAT's treatment in the return (recoverable against output, or restricted per the class) is ruled and configured on the accounts side; the procurement obligation is documents whose tax rows are computed by template and therefore usable by the return.

2. Withholding, located. Withholding tax applies at payment against the supplier's ruling (module 1's field) — it is a payment-time deduction, not an order-time charge: the order and invoice state the supplier's full claim; the payment entry withholds per the ruling and remits per the calendar. The location matters because withholding entered as an order discount misstates both the commitment and the statutory record.

3. Supplier advances. Where the arrangement's terms require payment before delivery (import lines commonly do; the domestic 30-day terms do not):

1. The advance is the terms' row — stated on the order's payment schedule as negotiated, per the same schedule machinery as the selling side.
2. The Payment Entry records it against the Purchase Order — the advance held against the supplier, visible on the ledger.
3. The allocation completes at invoicing — the advance applies against the invoice per the schedule; the unallocated-advances read (the payables mirror of the selling side's weekly read) lists advances without allocations to zero.
4. The exposure is real — an advance is the business's money in the supplier's hands before goods exist: the policy bands advance approvals accordingly, and the advance-exposure read lists outstanding advances by supplier with ages, because a supplier holding aged advances is a risk figure the review reads.

4. The commitment's currency. Foreign-currency orders carry the exposure module 1 stated: the order commits in the supplier's currency; the naira value moves until payment. The order file notes the exposure window per module 2's worksheet, and the accountant's revaluation machinery handles the ledger — the procurement contribution is, as everywhere, honest documents in true currencies.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The order book reads
lessons.html:
The open orders are the business's committed inbound supply. This chapter is the reads that keep the book true and worked.

1. The order book — weekly. All open orders with value, age, %received, %billed, and next scheduled date: the committed-money view (Chapter 3.5) and the working list, passed top-down by value with the largest commitments' next dates confirmed.

2. The incoming planning read — weekly (Chapter 4.3, restated as the book's column). Due, overdue, and at-risk rows, each with its ladder step and owner. The read's output feeds three consumers: the receiving dock's workload (module 6), the selling side's availability picture, and the chase ladder's worklist.

3. The received-not-billed read — weekly. Receipts whose invoices have not arrived or posted within the cadence: goods the business holds against a claim not yet stated. The list is worked two ways — the supplier chased for the invoice (the payables position cannot be planned from missing claims), and the accrual side handed to the accountant at period end per the Accounts track's procedures. Module 7 owns the matching; this read is its feeder.

4. The billed-not-received read — weekly. The inverse: invoices claiming goods the dock has not received. Legitimate cases trace to their structure (the advance invoice per the arrangement's schedule); the remainder are matching exceptions worked before payment — the read exists because paying claims ahead of goods is the exposure the three-way match guards, and module 7 details the control.

5. The stale-order hygiene — monthly. Open orders with no movement across the policy window: each revived with a confirmed schedule (the supplier re-commits dates by amendment) or Closed with its reason, releasing incoming. The cost of staleness is stated plainly: a stale order holds incoming quantity that suppresses the reorder engine — the trigger that should fire does not, because projected quantity includes an arrival that will never come. The hygiene read is therefore a stock-out prevention, not bookkeeping.

6. The cancellations and closures read — quarterly. The quarter's cancelled and closed orders by reason code: supplier-failure concentrations routed to the module 8 review and the split-award decisions; demand-ceased patterns routed to module 3's screening quality. Data with names, per the standing rule.

7. The filing. The order file per order — the demand trace, the award reference, the confirmation, the amendments, the drops, the receipts and invoices as they arrive — accumulates to the one-lookup standard, and modules 6-7 write the performance onto it.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the 300-carton Emzor order
lessons.html:
This chapter commits the purchase modules 3-4 prepared. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — creation from the consolidation (Chapter 2). The Purchase Order creates against the consolidated demand: supplier Emzor (the header pulling naira, 30-day terms, the named sales contact); one item — PARA-500 — structured as two rows for the two drops: 180 cartons required next week, 120 cartons the week after, both rows to Central Warehouse; the rate ₦9,600 per Carton-12 drawing from the arrangement, its source the module 4 decision minute. The Material Request links carry: the Central trigger's 260, Ibadan's 15, Akure's 25 — %ordered advances on all three at submission.

Step 2 — the pairing and the band confirmed (Chapters 2, 4). The pre-submission verification reads the rows: quantity-unit-rate paired (cartons against the carton rate throughout); the two-row total of 300 confirmed at the arrangement's volume band — one order, one commercial commitment, the band rate holding across both drops, which two separate 180- and 120-carton orders would each have missed.

Step 3 — submission and its effects (Chapter 3). The taxes compute per the purchase template (the exempt pharmaceutical class per its item treatment); the approval reviews the commitment against the award and the band; submission enters 300 cartons into Central's incoming — projected quantity rises above the reorder level, and the auto-trigger stands down: the engine sees the pipeline and does not order twice for one gap. The order transmits to Emzor's sales contact; the confirmation returns accepting quantities, the band rate, and both drop dates — the schedule is now the supplier's stated commitment, filed on the order.

Step 4 — the book carries it (Chapter 7). The weekly order book shows the commitment at value with its two dates; the incoming planning read places drop one in the coming window — the receiving dock (module 6) plans for 180 cartons; the selling side's availability picture includes the arrival. %received and %billed sit at zero, ready to advance per drop.

Step 5 — the money side, stated (Chapter 6). No advance applies — the 30-day terms mean the invoice for each drop will fall due thirty days after its date, and the payables due profile extends accordingly: the two drops spread the payable exactly as the multi-drop structure intends. Withholding does not apply to the goods class per the ruling; the input-VAT side is the exempt class's configured treatment — the money side of this order is therefore entirely the matching and payment machinery modules 6-7 will execute.

The handoff. The order file stands complete: three requests, the worksheet, the award minute, the order with two confirmed drops, the trace live in both directions. Drop one — 180 cartons, next week — is module 6's receiving case, where the dock discipline, the identity capture, and the 177-sound-3-crushed receipt await.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in Purchase Orders, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — the order without its demand. Symptom: orders raised from conversations; no requests behind the rows; the trace audit finding orphans. Correction: the demand recorded and screened retroactively where genuine. Prevention: creation from the consolidation or requests, and the gate configuration where the site enforces it.

Error 2 — the adjusted rate. Symptom: order rates edited away from their sources to match a supplier's ask or an invoice's claim; the award governance bypassed; matching comparing a document to itself. Correction: the rate restored to its source; the change routed through the arrangement's amendment or the matching exception. Prevention: rates carry sources, and differences are questions answered before submission.

Error 3 — the unconfirmed schedule. Symptom: orders transmitted into silence; dates the supplier never committed to; on-time measurement against hopes. Correction: confirmations chased through the read. Prevention: confirmation as part of the order procedure, and the unconfirmed-rows flag in the planning read.

Error 4 — the late submission. Symptom: consolidations decided but orders unsubmitted; the reorder trigger still armed and firing again; double demand in the pipeline. Correction: the duplicate demand stopped; the window's discipline restored. Prevention: the buying window closes with orders submitted, not worksheets approved.

Error 5 — the stale order suppressing the trigger. Symptom: incoming quantity from orders that will never arrive; projected figures above reorder levels; the stock-out arriving with the trigger silent. Correction: the hygiene read — revive with confirmed dates or Close with reason. Prevention: the monthly stale-order read, treated as stock-out prevention.

Error 6 — withholding as a discount. Symptom: withholding deducted on the order or invoice figures; the commitment and the statutory record both misstated. Correction: the documents restated at full claim; withholding relocated to payment per the ruling. Prevention: the location rule — orders and invoices state the full claim; payment withholds.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the field walk with the trace, sourced rates, per-row dates, and warehouses; state submission's effects on projected quantity and the execution basis, and what submission does not do; structure multi-drop schedules with the band-across-the-order rule and run the chase ladder; route changes by the taxonomy through the controlled lanes; configure the purchase tax side, locate withholding at payment, and manage advances with their exposure read; and run the order book's six reads.

Module rule 5: the Purchase Order states the whole purchase — created from screened demand at sourced rates, scheduled per row as the confirmed plan, committing the incoming figures at submission, changed only through the taxonomy's lanes, its taxes computed and its advances controlled — and kept live by the book's reads so the trigger, the dock, and the match all compute from truth. Module 6 covers Purchase Receipts.

receiving.title: Procurement 6 — Purchase Receipts & Quality: Goods In
receiving.desc: Purchase Receipts and the receiving function in ZhiftERP: the field walk — honest arrival dates, received quantities as counted, the accepted/rejected split, untouched order rates, and identity capture per manufacturing lot; the dock discipline — the expected-arrivals plan, the physical count against the order and the note, condition inspection with signed at-truck findings, the expiry gate, and the fixed sequence while the driver is present; the rejected lane with the three resolution lanes and the claims file; what submission posts — stock to two destinations at the receipt's rate, the projected transition, batch balances, and received-not-billed; quality holds and release by decision for the classes that require them; and the six receiving reads including the monthly performance figures feeding the supplier scorecards.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Receipt: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Purchase Receipt and the receiving function in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Purchase Receipt field walk; run the dock discipline — counting, damage identification, and identity capture at the truck; operate the accepted and rejected lanes with the supplier claim procedure; state what submission posts to stock and accounting; run quality holds and release for the classes that require them; and run the receiving reads.

What a Purchase Receipt is. The Purchase Receipt records a physical arrival of goods: which items, in what quantities, from which supplier's despatch, into which warehouse, on which date — with what came damaged, what identity numbers arrived, and who counted. It is the inbound custody-transfer document: before submission the goods are the supplier's despatch; after submission they are the business's stock at the receipt's figures. It is also the middle document of the three-way match — ordered, received, billed — and the matching control (module 7) is only as good as the receipt's honesty.

Position in the flow. The receipt sits between the Purchase Order and the Purchase Invoice:

1. Created against the order — the receipt draws the order's rows and receives against them: %received advances per row, incoming falls, and the trace runs order → receipt.
2. Feeding the match — the invoice (module 7) compares to the order's rates and the receipt's quantities; the receipt states what the business actually holds and therefore what claims it should accept.
3. Feeding stock — submission posts the goods into the warehouse at the receipt's figures, with the identity the recall trace and expiry management run on (the Inventory track consumes what this module captures).

The one-sentence standard. The standing rule the whole module serves: the receipt states what physically arrived — counted at the dock, split by condition, identified by lot, dated when it happened — never what the paperwork says should have arrived. The supplier's delivery note and the business's order are the references the count is compared against; the receipt records the count.

Custody. The receiving function counts and posts; the dock procedure requires the driver's presence through the count for disputed-at-truck findings; quality holds run per the class rules with the compliance owner's release; claims against suppliers file with their evidence; and receipts post on the day goods arrive, per the honest-date rule.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: the dock discipline. Chapter 4: accepted and rejected. Chapter 5: what submission posts. Chapter 6: quality and release. Chapter 7: the receiving reads. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Purchase Receipt doctype
lessons.html:
Create the Purchase Receipt from the Purchase Order (Create > Purchase Receipt) so the rows and references carry. Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Supplier and the order reference. Carried by creation; the supplier's delivery note number enters the reference field — the document the count was compared against, and the number every claim and query cites.

2. Posting Date and Time. When the goods physically arrived. The honest-date rule in its inbound form: the receipt posts on arrival day — a receipt posted days later carries stock the shelf held unrecorded (counts fail against it) and delays the received-not-billed accrual the accountant reads.

3. The items table. Per row, drawn from the order:

1. Received Quantity — what the dock counted, in the row's unit, per the pairing rule (cartons counted against carton rows). The received figure may be less than ordered (the short receipt), and the row records what arrived.
2. Accepted and Rejected Quantities — the condition split from the dock decision (Chapter 3): the received quantity divides into accepted (into the stock warehouse) and rejected (into the rejected warehouse), and the two fields post to their two destinations.
3. Warehouse and Rejected Warehouse — the accepted destination per the row (Central in the standing pattern), and the rejected lane's warehouse (the quarantine or rejected location the site names).
4. Rate — carried from the order. The receipt does not negotiate: a supplier's price change is a matching matter (module 7) or an arrangement amendment (module 4), never a receiving-time edit — the receipt's rate is the order's rate so the match has its reference.
5. Serial and batch capture — controlled items enter with their identity: the batch numbers and expiry dates on the physical cartons, the serial numbers on serialised units, per the Inventory track's dock rules. The identity captured here is what the recall trace, the expiry horizons, and the warranty records run on for the stock's whole life.

4. Save, verify, submit. The receipt is completed at the dock while the delivery is present, verified against the count sheets, and submitted on the day. Submission posts the stock and accounting events (Chapter 5); corrections after submission follow the document rules — the same physically-moved test as every custody document: cancellation only where the posting was wholly wrong on the day, the return-to-supplier lane where goods must physically go back.

Verification per receipt. The order and delivery-note references; the honest date; received quantities as counted; the accepted/rejected split per the dock decision; identity complete on controlled rows; rates untouched from the order.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The dock discipline
lessons.html:
The receiving procedure at the truck. Each step has an owner and a record, and the sequence is fixed because each step protects the next.

1. Before the truck: the expected-arrivals plan. The weekly incoming read (module 5) gives the dock its plan: what is due, in what quantities, with what identity requirements. A delivery nobody expected is itself a flag — checked against the order book before unloading, because unordered goods are either a supplier error or the beginning of an invoice for goods nobody bought.

2. The count. Goods count at the dock, physically, before the driver leaves:

1. Against the order and the delivery note — the two references; the count is the fact. Cartons count as cartons with sample-opening per the policy (the class's sampling rate: sealed manufacturer cartons sample-open; mixed or repacked consignments open fully).
2. In the row's units — the pairing rule at its origin point: the count sheet records quantity and unit together, and the carton-versus-unit confusion that mis-posts receipts is prevented here or nowhere.
3. Recorded on the count sheet — the physical record the receipt is entered from, filed with the receipt.

3. The condition inspection. While the driver is present: visible damage identified carton by carton — crushed, wet, broken seals, temperature indicators where the class carries them. Damaged units are set aside and counted separately: they become the rejected quantity (Chapter 4), and the finding is recorded on the driver's copy of the delivery note, signed by both parties — the at-truck record that makes the supplier claim a documented fact rather than a later assertion. Photographs per the claims procedure.

4. Identity capture. For controlled items, at the dock, from the physical cartons:

1. Batch numbers and expiry dates — read from the manufacturer's printing, entered per lot: a consignment carrying two manufacturing lots enters as two batch lines, each with its own expiry, because mixing lots into one line destroys the recall trace at its source.
2. The expiry gate — arriving expiry dates check against the policy's minimum-remaining-life rule: stock arriving with less than the class's required horizon is a rejection or a documented commercial decision, made now at the dock, not discovered at the shelf.
3. Serial capture — serialised units scanned or recorded individually, per the Inventory rules.

5. The driver's departure. The driver leaves with the signed delivery note stating what was received and what was disputed — quantities confirmed, damage noted, shortages recorded. After the truck leaves, the business's evidence is whatever was signed; the discipline's fixed sequence exists because every later conversation with the supplier is conducted from this document.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Accepted and rejected
lessons.html:
The received quantity divides by condition at the dock. This chapter is the two lanes and the claim procedure.

1. The accepted lane. Sound goods, in date per the expiry gate, matching the order: the accepted quantity posts into the stock warehouse at submission and becomes sellable inventory (or enters the quality hold first, where the class requires it — Chapter 6).

2. The rejected lane. Damaged, out-of-specification, or expiry-gate failures: the rejected quantity posts into the rejected warehouse — a named location whose stock is visibly not sellable, mirroring the quarantine pattern the Inventory track defined. The rejected lane's rules:

1. Rejected stock is held, not hidden — it remains on the books at the rejected location until its resolution, because goods physically present must be recorded present, whatever their condition.
2. Resolution by one of three lanes — return to the supplier (the return document per the site's flow, the physical send-back recorded), replacement (the supplier's replacement receiving as its own arrival, cross-referenced), or the credit claim (the rejected goods disposed per agreement, the credit note expected against the invoice — module 7's matching accounts for it).
3. Every rejection is a claim — raised with the supplier on the day, citing the signed delivery note and the photographs, with the resolution lane agreed and its deadline tracked by the open-claims read (Chapter 7).

3. Short receipts. The truck carries less than the delivery note states, or the note states less than the order: the receipt records what arrived (the standing rule), the shortage is noted on the signed copy, and the order row remains open for the balance — the supplier delivers the remainder, or the order amends per module 5's taxonomy with the shortfall's cause recorded. What never happens: receiving paper quantities to match documents — the receipt that records 180 because the note says 180 while the truck carried 177 corrupts stock, the match, and the claim in one act.

4. Over-receipts. The truck carries more than ordered: the over-receipt tolerance (the control-register setting, low, with the exception role named) admits genuine packing arithmetic; beyond it, the excess is refused at the dock or accepted only by the named role's decision with the order amended — unordered goods accepted casually become unmatched invoice lines and, repeated, a supplier habit.

5. The claims file. Per claim: the signed note, the photographs, the receipt's rejected line, the correspondence, the agreed lane, the resolution and its date. Claims are money — the rejected cartons are paid-for goods until the claim resolves — and the open-claims read works the file to zero with ages visible.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — What submission posts
lessons.html:
Submission converts the counted, split, identified receipt into stock and accounting events. This chapter states each posting.

1. The stock posting. Per row, Stock Ledger Entries: the accepted quantity into the stock warehouse, the rejected quantity into the rejected warehouse — both at the receipt's rate, because rejected goods are still the business's cost until their claim resolves. The Bins update; for controlled items, the batch and serial balances create with the captured identity — the lot lines, expiries, and serials entering the registers the Inventory track operates from this moment on.

2. The projected-quantity update. The received quantities leave the incoming figures: %received advances on the order rows; projected quantity converts its pipeline component into actual stock. The reorder machinery's arithmetic stays true through the transition — the arrival neither double-counts (incoming falling as actual rises) nor disappears.

3. The accounting posting. Under perpetual inventory: the stock account debits at the receipt's value, and the offsetting credit posts to the received-not-billed account — the liability that says goods are held whose invoice has not yet posted. When module 7's invoice posts, it clears this account against the supplier's payable: the two-step structure is what lets the books state, at any moment, both what stock the business holds and what claims it has accepted — separately and truthfully. The received-not-billed balance is therefore a working figure the accountant reads at each close, and the module 5 read that chases missing invoices keeps it short.

4. The valuation tie. The receipt's rate is the valuation's starting figure (module 2's third cost): domestic included-delivery lines are substantially complete at receipt; import lines gain their acquisition layer afterward through the Landed Cost Voucher (the Inventory mechanism), which re-rates the receipt's stock with the actual freight, duty, and clearing — the worksheet-versus-actual reconciliation from module 2 closing per consignment.

5. Corrections after submission. The lanes, per the physically-moved test:

1. The posting was wrong on the day (wrong warehouse selected, a count-sheet transcription error caught same-day): cancel and re-post with the honest figures, the reason recorded.
2. Goods must physically go back — the return-to-supplier lane: its own document recording the physical send-back, never a cancellation of an arrival that happened.
3. The identity was captured wrong (a batch number transposed): the correction per the Inventory track's identity procedures, because downstream documents may already reference the lot.

6. The tie-out participation. Receipt postings are part of the monthly stock-to-accounts agreement: a tie-out difference tracing to receiving is read through this chapter's postings — the stock entry, the received-not-billed entry, and the document, together.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Quality and release
lessons.html:
Some classes do not go straight to shelf. This chapter is the hold-and-release structure.

1. The quality hold pattern. Per the class rules the compliance owner maintains: classes requiring inspection before sale (temperature-sensitive lines, classes with regulatory release requirements, first receipts from new suppliers, trial orders per module 4's award conditions) receive into the quarantine warehouse rather than free stock:

1. The accepted-quantity posting targets quarantine for these classes — the goods are the business's stock, visible and counted, but not sellable.
2. The inspection runs per the class's procedure — the checks, the sampling, the documentation — by the roles the procedure names.
3. Release is a movement with a decision: the transfer from quarantine to free stock, posted by the release role, with the inspection record filed. Stock does not drift out of quarantine; it is released.

2. The pharmaceutical specifics. The standing case's class rules:

1. The expiry horizons — the dock gate (Chapter 3) enforced arrival life; the quarantine inspection confirms lot documentation where the class requires it (the manufacturer's certificates per the compliance file).
2. Cold-chain classes — the temperature record travels with the consignment; a broken indicator is a rejection at the dock or a quarantine-and-inspect decision per the procedure, never a shrug.
3. The compliance file per lot — the certificates, the inspection record, the release decision: the file the regulator, the recall procedure, and the customer complaint all read.

3. Failed inspections. The quarantined goods that fail: the rejection converts (the stock moves to the rejected lane), the claim raises per Chapter 4 with the inspection record as evidence, and the resolution lanes apply. A failure pattern by supplier or class is a scorecard fact (module 8's quality dimension) and, recurring, an award-criteria fact for the next cycle.

4. The hold reads. Weekly, with the receiving reads: quarantine contents by age against the class's release windows — stock aging in quarantine is either an inspection backlog (a resourcing question) or a forgotten release (a procedure question), and both are visible because quarantine is a warehouse the reads see, not a corner of the dock. The release records sample monthly with the receipt audit.

5. The boundary. The compliance owner rules which classes hold and what release requires; the receiving function routes per the rules; the Inventory track's quarantine machinery (module 1's warehouse, module 3's identity) is the infrastructure. This module's contribution is the inbound routing and the discipline that the rules are applied at the dock, every arrival, without judgment calls at the truck.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The receiving reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the receiving function, each with its cadence and action.

1. The expected-arrivals plan — weekly. Module 5's incoming read consumed as the dock's plan: due rows by day, quantities, identity requirements, and the unexpected-delivery rule standing (unordered arrivals checked before unloading).

2. The receipts-pending-invoice read — weekly. Module 5's received-not-billed read operated from the receiving side: submitted receipts whose invoices have not arrived within the cadence, the supplier chased for the claim, the accrual position handed to the accountant at close. The read feeds module 7's matching queue.

3. The open-claims read — weekly. Every unresolved rejection and shortage claim by age: the agreed lane, the deadline, the next action. Claims are worked to zero because each is paid-for goods (or short-delivered goods) awaiting money or replacement — the read's aging column is naira aging, and claims resolving by replacement track into the affected drops' schedules.

4. The receipt audit — monthly. A sample of the month's receipts checked for the discipline's evidence: posting dates against arrival dates (the honest-date check), count sheets attached, accepted/rejected splits with their signed notes where rejections occurred, identity complete on controlled rows (lots separated, expiries entered), rates untouched from orders. Findings correct the procedure or the training per the standing pattern, and the audit files with the month's records.

5. The receiving-performance figures — monthly, feeding module 8. Per supplier, from the receipts: on-time performance (arrival dates against confirmed dates, per drop), quantity fidelity (short and over receipts), and condition (rejection rates by cause). These figures are the scorecard's receiving-side inputs — measured at the dock, from documents, per the module 8 weightings — and the monthly compilation is where the dock's records become the relationship review's evidence.

6. The exception patterns — quarterly. The quarter's receiving exceptions aggregated: damage concentrated by supplier, route, or packaging (routed to the claims history and the carrier conversation), short-receipt patterns (routed to the supplier review), unexpected deliveries (routed to the order discipline), and quarantine aging (routed to the resourcing or procedure question). Data with names, filed with the quarterly cycle alongside the module 8 scorecard compilation.

Why the three reads sit together. Each one closes a different gap between the physical world and the records: goods arriving nobody expected, goods received nobody billed, and claims raised nobody resolved. All three are cheap in the week they appear and expensive in the quarter they accumulate — an unresolved claim ages into an assertion, and an unbilled receipt becomes an accrual the accountant cannot evidence.
