lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: drop one arrives
lessons.html:
This chapter receives the first drop of the module 5 order: 180 cartons of PARA-500 from Emzor, due this week at Central Warehouse. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the plan and the truck (Chapter 3). The expected-arrivals plan carries the drop: 180 cartons, batch-controlled, expiry-gated. The truck arrives with Emzor's delivery note stating 180; the dock counts against the note and the order.

Step 2 — the count and the condition split (Chapters 3-4). The physical count: 180 cartons on the truck — 177 sound, 3 crushed at the bottom of one stack. The damage is identified while the driver is present: the three cartons set aside, photographed, and recorded on the driver's copy of the delivery note, signed by both parties — 180 received, 3 damaged noted. The count sheet records quantities in cartons throughout, per the pairing rule.

Step 3 — identity capture (Chapter 3). The consignment carries two manufacturing lots, and the dock enters them as two batch lines with their printed expiry dates — one of them batch B-1147, the lot whose register entry the Inventory track's recall procedures will later exercise. Both lots pass the expiry gate with the class's required horizon remaining. The two-lot separation is the recall trace's foundation: one blended line here would have made the later lot-level freeze impossible to execute cleanly.

Step 4 — the receipt posts (Chapters 2, 5). The Purchase Receipt creates from the order's first row: received 180, accepted 177 into Central, rejected 3 into the rejected warehouse, both at the order's ₦9,600 carton rate; the delivery-note reference and count sheet attach; the posting date is arrival day. Submission posts the stock entries (177 sellable at Central; 3 held visible at rejected), creates the two batch balances with expiries, advances %received on the order (177 of 300 net of the claim's outcome), converts the drop's incoming into actual — the auto-trigger's arithmetic staying true — and posts the received-not-billed liability the invoice will clear.

Step 5 — the claim (Chapter 4). The claim raises with Emzor the same day: the signed note, the photographs, the receipt's rejected line. The agreed lane: replacement — three cartons added to drop two, which amends per module 5's schedule taxonomy from 120 to 123 with the reason recorded and Emzor's confirmation updated. The claims file tracks the resolution; the rejected three remain visible at the rejected warehouse until the return-or-dispose step the agreement states, and the open-claims read carries the item until closed.

Step 6 — the figures file (Chapter 7). The month's receiving-performance compilation records the drop: on time against its confirmed date; 180 of 180 quantity fidelity; a 1.7%-of-drop damage entry by cause (transit crush) — the figures module 8's scorecard will weigh. The receipt audit's sample later confirms the discipline's evidence complete: honest date, count sheet, signed note, two lots separated, rates untouched.

The handoff. Drop two — now 123 cartons — holds its confirmed date; Emzor's invoice for drop one is en route to module 7's three-way match, where 177 accepted cartons at ₦9,600, a 3-carton claim, and a 180-carton invoice will meet the matching discipline.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in receiving, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — receiving the paperwork. Symptom: receipts entered from delivery notes without counting; the note's 180 posted while the truck carried 177; stock, the match, and the claim corrupted in one act. Correction: the physical position re-established by count; the documents corrected through their lanes. Prevention: the count as the fact, the note as the reference — the module's one-sentence standard.

Error 2 — the driver gone before the record. Symptom: damage and shortages discovered after departure; claims reduced to assertions; suppliers declining undocumented findings. Correction: the claim attempted on the evidence that exists. Prevention: the fixed dock sequence — count, inspect, record, sign — completed while the driver is present.

Error 3 — blended lots. Symptom: multi-lot consignments entered as one batch line; expiries averaged or guessed; the recall trace broken at its source. Correction: the identity corrected per the Inventory procedures while the physical separation is still known. Prevention: one batch line per manufacturing lot, entered from the printed cartons at the dock.

Error 4 — the rate edited at receiving. Symptom: receipt rates changed to match a supplier's new price or an expected invoice; the match comparing a document to itself; the award governance bypassed at the dock. Correction: the rate restored; the price question routed to matching or the arrangement. Prevention: the receipt carries the order's rate, without exception.

Error 5 — the invisible rejection. Symptom: damaged goods set aside physically but not posted; stock the books do not show; claims never raised; the pile by the dock door that every warehouse accumulates. Correction: the rejected stock posted, claims raised on surviving evidence. Prevention: the accepted/rejected split on the receipt itself, and rejected as a warehouse the reads see.

Error 6 — the drifting quarantine. Symptom: held stock leaking to shelf without release decisions; inspection backlogs invisible; the compliance file incomplete. Correction: the quarantine reconciled, releases documented retroactively where defensible. Prevention: release as a posted movement with a decision, and the weekly hold read.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the receipt walk with honest dates, the condition split, untouched rates, and identity per lot; run the dock sequence — plan, count, inspect, capture, sign — while the driver is present; operate the rejected lane with the three resolution lanes and the claims file; state the postings — stock to two destinations, the projected transition, received-not-billed — and the correction lanes; route quality-hold classes and release by decision; and run the six receiving reads.

Module rule 6: the receipt states what physically arrived — counted at the dock against the order and the note, split by condition with the driver's signature on the findings, identified lot by lot from the cartons, posted at the order's rate on the arrival day, held visibly where rejected or quarantined, and claimed with evidence until every rejection resolves. Module 7 covers the Purchase Invoice and the three-way match.

purchase_invoice.title: Procurement 7 — Purchase Invoices, Payments & the Nigerian Frame
purchase_invoice.desc: The Purchase Invoice, the three-way match, and the payables machinery in ZhiftERP: the field walk — exact supplier numbering, computed due dates, entry as claimed, and the hold facility; the three comparisons — billed not exceeding accepted, invoice rates equal to order rates with the pairing read, and the tax and arithmetic checks; the exception taxonomy with its lanes and the closes-with-a-document rule; posting effects — the payable, received-not-billed clearing, input VAT, and the due-date machinery; the weekly payment run on terms with line-by-line allocation, withholding at payment with the remittance calendar, and the verified-account rule; debit notes, credit notes, and replacement resolutions with the claim-to-clearing reconciliation; and the six payables reads including the monthly statement reconciliation.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The Purchase Invoice: scope and position
lessons.html:
This module covers the Purchase Invoice, the three-way match, and the payables machinery in ZhiftERP. On completing this module you will be able to: complete the Purchase Invoice field walk; run the three-way match and state what each comparison checks; work the matching exceptions through their lanes; state what posting creates and clears; operate the payment run with withholding at payment; clear claims through debit notes and credits; and run the payables reads.

What a Purchase Invoice is. The Purchase Invoice records the supplier's claim: the demand for payment for goods or services, at stated rates, with stated taxes, due on a computable date. Posting it recognises the claim in the books — the payable exists from posting, not from payment — and the discipline of this module is that a claim is recognised only after it has been compared to what was ordered and what was received. The comparison is the three-way match, and it is the buying side's principal money control: the business pays for what it agreed to buy and actually holds, at the rates it agreed, and nothing else.

Position in the flow. The invoice is the third document:

1. The order (module 5) stated the agreement — quantities, rates, terms.
2. The receipt (module 6) stated the arrival — counted, split by condition.
3. The invoice states the claim — and posts only when the claim reconciles to the other two, or when its exceptions have been worked to documented resolutions.

Why the sequence protects the money. Each upstream document was built precisely so this comparison would work: the order's rates carry sources (a claim above them is visible), the receipt's counts are physical (a claim beyond them is visible), and the exceptions that surface here are therefore findings with evidence rather than arguments about memory. A business that pays invoices without the match is trusting every supplier's paperwork with its bank balance.

Custody. The payables function enters and matches invoices; exceptions resolve through their lanes with the roles each lane names; posting approval per the matrix; payment runs on the calendar with the verified-account rule (module 1); and the standing rule: the supplier is paid what the match supports, on the terms agreed, to the account verified — every difference worked as a documented exception, never absorbed by editing a document to make it pass.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the field walk. Chapter 3: the three-way match. Chapter 4: matching exceptions. Chapter 5: what posting does. Chapter 6: payments and withholding. Chapter 7: debit notes and claims clearing. Chapter 8: the payables reads. Chapter 9: worked example. Chapter 10: review and the module rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Purchase Invoice doctype
lessons.html:
Create the Purchase Invoice from the Purchase Receipt or Purchase Order (Create > Purchase Invoice) so the rows and references carry. Complete or verify the fields in order.

1. Supplier and the references. The supplier per the register; the order and receipt references carried by creation — the match's connective tissue, and the reason invoices enter from their documents rather than from blank forms.

2. The supplier's invoice number and date. Entered exactly as printed: the supplier's numbering is the statutory identity of the claim — the number the supplier's statement will cite, the tax records reference, and the duplicate check runs on. The system's duplicate detection works on this field: the same supplier number entered twice is the double-payment attempt (or error) caught at entry, and the field's accuracy is what makes the check work.

3. Posting date and due date. The posting date per the accountant's period rules; the due date computes from the payment terms — the negotiated 30 days running from the terms' reference date. The due date is machinery, not a note: the payment run (Chapter 6) selects by it, the cash forecast (Chapter 8) profiles by it, and editing it by hand outside a documented terms change misstates the payable's timing.

4. The items table. Per row, carried from the receipt or order: item, quantity, rate, the warehouse or expense context per the accountant's design. The rows are what the match compares (Chapter 3); they are verified against the supplier's printed invoice — the entry states the supplier's claim as made, and the match then judges it. The entry does not pre-correct the claim to what it should have been: an invoice claiming 180 is entered claiming 180, and the exception lane handles the difference, because a pre-corrected entry destroys the record of what the supplier actually claimed.

5. Taxes and Charges. The purchase tax template computing the claim's tax rows; the supplier's printed tax figures compared to the computed figures — a difference is a tax exception (Chapter 4), commonly a rate or classification error on one side, resolved before posting because the input-VAT records must state the claim correctly.

6. The hold facility. An entered invoice that cannot yet post — an unworked exception, a missing receipt, an awaited credit — holds explicitly: on the queue with its reason, visible to the reads, rather than in a drawer. The hold is the honest state between arrival and resolution, and the disputed-invoices read (Chapter 8) works the held list by age.

Verification per invoice. References carried; the supplier's number and date exact; the due date computed from terms; rows as claimed; taxes compared; then to the match.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The three-way match
lessons.html:
The match compares the claim to the agreement and the arrival. This chapter is each comparison and its standard.

1. The quantity match. Billed quantity per row against the received accepted quantity:

1. The standard: billed does not exceed accepted. The business pays for goods it holds as sound stock. Rejected quantities are not payable as delivered goods — they are claims in progress (module 6), and their money resolves through the claim's lane (Chapter 7), not through paying the full invoice and hoping.
2. Billed below accepted is the partial invoice — legitimate where the supplier bills in parts; the remainder stays received-not-billed until claimed.
3. The multi-receipt case — one invoice covering several receipts matches against their sum; the references list every receipt.

2. The rate match. The invoice's rate per row against the order's rate:

1. The standard: the invoice rate equals the order rate. The order's rate carries the award's authority (module 4); a claim above it is an exception, whatever the supplier's cover letter says — the price conversation happens in the arrangement's governance, not on an invoice.
2. The pairing rule at the match — rate variances that are really unit variances (the carton rate against a unit line) are the first check, per the standing discipline: the classic false variance, resolved by reading quantity-unit-rate together on both documents.

3. The tax match. The supplier's tax arithmetic against the template's computation: the VAT base, the rate applied, exempt lines treated as exempt. Differences are corrected on whichever side is wrong — the supplier's corrected invoice, or the entry's template selection — before posting, because the return compiles from these rows.

4. The arithmetic match. Extensions and totals recomputed: quantity times rate per row, the tax on the correct base, the total as the sum. Suppliers' systems err rarely; typed invoices err more; the check costs a minute per invoice and the recomputation is part of the entry verification.

5. The match as comparison. Because the upstream documents were kept honest, the match is mechanical: three figures per row — ordered, accepted, billed — and two rates — agreed and claimed. An invoice that matches posts the same day (Chapter 5); an invoice that does not becomes an exception with the evidence already on file: the order's sourced rate, the receipt's signed count, the claim's photographs. The match never edits a document to force agreement — the difference is the finding, and the finding routes (Chapter 4).

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Matching exceptions
lessons.html:
Differences route through defined lanes. This chapter is the exception taxonomy and the queue.

1. Quantity exceptions. Billed exceeds accepted:

1. The rejected-goods case — the invoice claims the full despatch while the receipt rejected part of it (the standing case: 180 claimed, 177 accepted, 3 rejected with a claim on file). The resolution follows the claim's agreed lane: the supplier issues a corrected invoice or a credit note for the rejected portion, or — where the agreed lane is replacement — the commercial arithmetic settles across the drops per the agreement, documented on both files. The invoice holds, or posts at the supported figure per the site's procedure, with the difference tracked to the claim's resolution — never paid in full on the promise that it will sort itself out.
2. The never-received case — the invoice claims goods no receipt shows: the billed-not-received read's territory (module 5), held until the goods arrive, the receipt posts, or the claim withdraws.
3. The duplicate — the same claim twice under two numbers: the duplicate check and the statement reconciliation both catch it; the second claim is rejected with the first's reference.

2. Rate exceptions. The claimed rate differs from the order's:

1. Checked against the arrangement first — a price change with a dated amendment (module 4) means the order should have been amended: the governance gap is noted, the documents align to the amendment, the invoice posts at the amended rate.
2. No amendment — the claim is declined at the difference: the supplier corrects the invoice, or the difference escalates to the relationship level with the award file as the record. The rate the business pays is the rate it agreed.

3. Tax and arithmetic exceptions. Per Chapter 3: corrected on the erring side before posting; recurring tax errors from one supplier are a scorecard note and a conversation.

4. The exception queue. Every exception enters the queue with its type, age, value, and owner: the held invoices, the awaited credits, the escalated rates. The queue works on the weekly cadence — exceptions age into the disputed read (Chapter 8) — and the rule that keeps the queue honest: an exception closes with a document — the corrected invoice, the credit note, the amendment, the withdrawal — never with a shrug and a posting. The quarterly exception pattern (types by supplier) files with the scorecard inputs: a supplier whose invoices routinely claim above receipts or rates is a measured fact for the module 8 review.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — What posting does
lessons.html:
The matched invoice posts. This chapter states each effect.

1. The payable. Posting credits the supplier's payable at the claim's total: the liability exists in the books from this moment, due on the computed date. The supplier's ledger — every invoice, payment, and debit note in one view — is the account the statement reconciliation (Chapter 8) agrees, and the payables aging (Chapter 8) buckets.

2. Received-not-billed clears. For stock invoices, posting clears the receipt's received-not-billed liability against the payable (module 6's two-step completing): the goods-held-awaiting-claim state converts to a stated debt. The received-not-billed balance falls by the matched receipt's value, and the residual balance — receipts still awaiting invoices — remains the accountant's accrual figure at close.

3. The input-VAT record. The tax rows post to the input-VAT accounts per the template's heads: the claim's VAT, stated correctly, enters the records the accountant's return compiles from. The procurement obligation ends where it always ends — documents whose tax rows are computed and matched; the return's arithmetic and the recoverability rulings are the accounts side's work.

4. The cost tie. Stock invoices at matched rates confirm the receipt's valuation (rate variances that survived to posting adjust per the accountant's configuration — the valuation machinery the Inventory track owns); expense invoices land on their expense heads and cost contexts per the accountant's design. The module's contribution to costing is the match itself: invoices posting at agreed rates is what keeps the module 2 cost figures meaning what they claim.

5. The due-date machinery engages. The posted payable enters the due profile: the payment run (Chapter 6) will select it by date; the cash forecast (Chapter 8) carries it; the terms the business negotiated (module 4) now operate as working capital exactly as intended — the 30-day term is thirty days of the supplier financing the stock, used fully and honoured precisely.

6. Corrections after posting. The lanes: the supplier's own correction instruments (their corrected invoice or credit note) enter as their documents against the ledger; the business-side error (wrong template, wrong context) corrects per the accountant's amendment rules with the reason recorded. The claim record's integrity holds throughout — what the supplier claimed, what was recognised, what corrected it, each on its own document.

The posting that surprises people the first time. Received-not-billed does not clear because the invoice arrived — it clears because the invoice posted, and an invoice held in the exception queue leaves the accrual standing. That is correct behaviour: the goods are held and the claim is disputed, so the liability is stated as an accrual rather than as an agreed debt. Anybody reading a stubborn received-not-billed balance at close should look at the exception queue first.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Payments and withholding
lessons.html:
Posted payables pay on the calendar. This chapter is the payment machinery.

1. The payment run — weekly. The run selects posted invoices due within the window, per the standing posture (module 1): on terms, neither early nor late — early payment surrenders negotiated working capital; late payment spends the relationship and the terms' credibility at the next negotiation. The run's list reviews per the matrix (the approver sees supplier, invoices, amounts, and accounts), and exceptions to the posture — the early-payment discount worth taking, the withheld payment on a disputed account — are decisions recorded on the run, not habits.

2. The Payment Entry. Per supplier per run: the payment against its invoices, allocated line by line — the supplier's ledger shows which claims this payment settles. The allocation discipline mirrors the receivables side: payments without allocations age on the unallocated read (Chapter 8) and are resolved with the supplier's advice, because an unallocated payment makes the ledger unable to state which invoices remain open.

3. Withholding at payment. Where the supplier's ruling requires it (module 1's field, per the accountant's determination):

1. The deduction computes at the Payment Entry — the statutory percentage on the ruled base: the supplier receives the net; the withheld amount posts to the remittance liability.
2. The invoice stated the full claim — the location rule from module 5: orders and invoices at full value; the payment withholds. The supplier's ledger then shows claim, payment, and withholding distinctly, which is what the supplier's own reconciliation and the statutory credit note require.
3. The remittance calendar — withheld amounts remit to the authority per the accountant's schedule, with the supplier's evidence (the credit documentation) issued per the procedure. Withholding held and not remitted is a statutory liability aging in the books; the remittance read keeps it current.

4. The verified-account rule. Payments go only to bank details verified per module 1's call-back procedure — the run's final check, every run, because the emailed account-change fraud targets exactly this moment. A change surfacing inside the run window is a stopped payment and a verification, never a convenience edit.

5. Partial payments and advances. Partial payments allocate to their invoices with the balance visibly open; advances from module 5 allocate at posting per the schedule, closing the advance-exposure entries. The supplier's ledger states the whole position — claims, payments, advances, withholdings — and the weekly run works from it.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Debit notes and claims clearing
lessons.html:
The receiving claims (module 6) resolve in money or replacement. This chapter is the clearing machinery.

1. The instruments.

1. The supplier's credit note — the supplier's document reducing their claim: entered against the ledger, referencing the original invoice and the claim, offsetting the payable. The standing resolution for damage and shortage claims settling in money.
2. The debit note — the business-side instrument (the return-flagged purchase document per the site's flow) recording goods returned to the supplier or charges back per agreement: posted with its references, reducing the payable, matching the physical return document where goods moved.
3. The replacement — no money instrument: the supplier's replacement goods receive as their own arrival (module 6), cross-referenced to the claim, and the commercial arithmetic across the affected drops documents on both files — the standing case's lane.

2. The claim-to-clearing reconciliation. Every module 6 claim carries to its money or goods resolution:

1. The claims file states the agreed lane and deadline;
2. The clearing read (weekly, with the open-claims read) lists claims whose instruments have not arrived — the credit note promised but not issued is chased like the missing invoice, because until it posts the payable overstates;
3. Closure requires the pair: the claim's file and the ledger's instrument, cross-referenced. A claim closed without its instrument is money conceded silently.

3. Rejected-goods disposal ties. The rejected warehouse (module 6) empties as claims resolve: returned goods leave on the return document; goods the agreement lets the business dispose of leave per the write-off rules with the claim's reference. The rejected location's contents reconcile to open claims — stock there with no claim is an unraised claim; a claim with no stock and no resolution is a disposal that skipped its document. The weekly claims pass runs this reconciliation alongside the clearing read.

4. The supplier's ledger, complete. After this chapter the ledger states every instrument the relationship produces: invoices, payments, withholdings, advances, credit notes, debit notes — each referenced to its documents. The statement reconciliation (Chapter 8) agrees this ledger to the supplier's records monthly, and the one-lookup standard applies: any line's story — which order, which receipt, which claim, which resolution — answerable from its references.

Clearing claims is a discipline, not an event. A claim raised at the dock, agreed with the supplier, and then never converted into a credit note or a debit note leaves the money in nobody's column: the business believes it is owed something and the supplier's statement disagrees, and both are working from records that were correct when they were made. The clearing step is what turns an agreement into an entry, and the open-claims read exists because it is the step most often left undone.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The payables reads
lessons.html:
The standing reads on the payables position, each with its cadence and action.

1. The payables aging — weekly. Open payables by bucket: current, and overdue by age. The buying side ages differently from the receivables mirror — overdue payables are the business's own performance: each overdue line has a cause read from the ledger (a held exception, a missed run, a cash decision), and the causes route — exceptions to the queue, cash decisions to the owner's visibility, process misses to the run's discipline. The relationship cost of drifting payment is a scorecard the suppliers keep.

2. The due profile — weekly. Posted payables by due week, extended by the order book's committed values (module 5): the buying side's cash forecast, read with the receivables profile by the accountant and the owner. The profile is why due dates compute rather than type: a forecast built on hand-edited dates forecasts nothing.

3. The unallocated and advances read — weekly. Payments without full allocation, advances without invoice application: worked to zero per Chapters 5-6, because the ledger's open-invoice list is only true when allocations are complete.

4. The disputed and held read — weekly. The exception queue (Chapter 4) and held invoices by age and value: the money in dispute stated as a figure, each item with its next action and owner. Aging disputes escalate per the ladder — the relationship level, then the review — and the read's total is a working-capital figure the accountant watches, because disputed money is unplannable money.

5. The statement reconciliation — monthly. The supplier's statement against the ledger, per module 1's cadence: every line agreed or listed as a difference — the invoice the business never received (requested and matched), the payment the supplier has not applied (the remittance advice re-sent), the credit note promised and absent (the claims chase), the duplicate the statement exposes. The reconciliation is the payables function's completeness check: entry errors, lost documents, and silent differences surface here monthly rather than at year-end, and the reconciled statement files with the month's records.

6. The quarterly compilation. The quarter's payables figures file with the procurement records: exception patterns by supplier (Chapter 4), payment performance both ways (the business's own timeliness; the suppliers' credit-note responsiveness), and the withholding remittance record — the money side's contribution to the module 8 reviews and the owner's quarterly view.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Worked example: matching drop one
lessons.html:
This chapter matches and pays the standing case. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the claim arrives (Chapter 2). Emzor's invoice for drop one arrives: 180 cartons of PARA-500 at ₦9,600 — the full despatch as loaded, the supplier's numbering entered exactly, the due date computing thirty days from the terms' reference. The entry states the claim as made: 180 cartons, ₦1,728,000, the exempt class's tax treatment computing per template.

Step 2 — the match runs (Chapter 3). Per row: rate — ₦9,600 claimed against ₦9,600 ordered, the pairing read confirming cartons against the carton rate: rate match holds. Quantity — 180 billed against 177 accepted: the quantity match finds the 3-carton difference, and the receipt's file already holds the evidence — the signed delivery note, the photographs, the rejected line, the claim.

Step 3 — the exception works its lane (Chapter 4). The difference is the known claim, agreed as replacement (module 6): the resolution documents across the two files per the agreement — Emzor issues a corrected invoice for 177 cartons, ₦1,699,200, and the replacement three cartons carry to drop two's delivery and billing. The original entry cancels against the corrected claim with both numbers cross-referenced; the exception closes with its documents — the corrected invoice and the claim's confirmation — per the queue's rule.

Step 4 — posting (Chapter 5). The corrected invoice matches clean — 177 billed, 177 accepted, ₦9,600 both sides — and posts: the payable credits ₦1,699,200 due in thirty days; the receipt's received-not-billed clears by the matched value; the ledger opens the relationship's first invoice line with its order, receipt, and claim references. Withholding does not apply to the goods class per the ruling.

Step 5 — drop two completes the arithmetic (Chapters 3, 7). Drop two arrives per its amended schedule: 123 cartons — 120 ordered plus the 3 replacements — received clean, the claim closing on the replacement's arrival with both files cross-referenced. Emzor invoices 123 cartons, ₦1,180,800; the match holds (123 billed, 123 accepted, the band rate across the order per module 5); the invoice posts on its own thirty-day clock. The order completes: 300 cartons received sound, ₦2,880,000 billed across two invoices — the band's total arithmetic exact, the claim resolved in goods, nothing conceded silently.

Step 6 — payment and reconciliation (Chapters 6, 8). Each invoice pays in the run of its due week — on terms, neither early nor late — allocated to its line, to Emzor's verified account per the call-back file. The due profile carried both payables from posting; the month's statement reconciliation agrees Emzor's statement to the ledger line for line: two invoices, one cancelled-and-corrected pair cross-referenced, two payments, no differences.

The file evidence. Order, two receipts, the claim with its signed note, the corrected invoice pair, two clean matches, two on-terms payments, the reconciled statement — the whole purchase answerable from any line in one lookup, and the performance figures (on-time per drop, the 1.7% damage, the claim's resolution speed) filed for module 8's scorecard.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common errors and the module rule
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in purchase invoicing and payables, each with its correction and prevention.

Error 1 — paying without the match. Symptom: invoices posted and paid on arrival; claims above orders and receipts absorbed; the bank balance trusting supplier paperwork. Correction: the match imposed on open items; historic exposure sampled. Prevention: the match as the posting gate, and the exception queue for everything that fails it.

Error 2 — editing documents to force the match. Symptom: order rates adjusted to invoice claims, receipt quantities nudged to billed figures; the match comparing documents to themselves; the control formally present and actually gone. Correction: the documents restored to their sources; the differences reopened as exceptions. Prevention: the standing rule — the difference is the finding; it routes, it is never absorbed.

Error 3 — the pre-corrected entry. Symptom: invoices entered at what they should have claimed; the record of the supplier's actual claim destroyed; disputes unarguable. Correction: entries restated as claimed with exceptions attached. Prevention: enter as claimed, match, then route.

Error 4 — withholding on the invoice. Symptom: claims entered net of withholding; the statutory record and the supplier's ledger both misstated; remittance arithmetic wrong. Correction: full-claim restatement; withholding relocated to payment. Prevention: the location rule, per modules 5-6.

Error 5 — the silent claim concession. Symptom: claims closed without instruments; credit notes promised and never chased; rejected stock disposed without documents; the payable overstating and the money conceded. Correction: the claims file reconciled to the ledger; open items rechased. Prevention: closure requires the pair — the claim's file and the ledger's instrument.

Error 6 — the drifting run. Symptom: payments early by habit or late by neglect; working capital surrendered or the relationship spent; allocations skipped under time pressure. Correction: the posture restated; unallocated items worked. Prevention: the weekly run on terms with allocation as part of the entry, and the aging read's causes routed.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: complete the invoice walk with exact supplier numbering and computed due dates; run the three comparisons and state each standard; route the exception taxonomy through its lanes with the closes-with-a-document rule; state posting's effects on the payable, received-not-billed, and input VAT; operate the run on terms with withholding at payment and the verified-account check; clear claims through the three instruments with the reconciliation; and run the six payables reads.

Module rule 7: the supplier is paid what the match supports — the claim entered as made, compared to the order's agreed rates and the receipt's accepted counts, its differences worked as documented exceptions that close with instruments, posted to a ledger that states the whole relationship, and paid on terms to verified accounts through the weekly run. Module 8 covers supplier scorecards, buying-side agreements, and the procurement calendar.

advanced_buying.title: Procurement 8 — Advanced Buying: Settings, Scorecards & Structure
advanced_buying.desc: Advanced buying and the procurement calendar in ZhiftERP: supplier scorecards on the 40/35/25 weights — price competitiveness, per-drop on-time-in-full delivery, and quality from the condition and claims records — computed from document variables with weight governance; the standings ladder with stated actions, gates, and documented overrides, and the measured-conversation rule; tiered relationship reviews from assembled agendas to outcome minutes with payment performance read both ways; buying-side blanket orders distinguished from rate arrangements, with call-offs, the consumption read, and expiry as negotiation; the subcontracting flow — service-rate orders, the subcontractor warehouse, assembled valuation, and the reconciliation cadence; Buying Settings as control-register rows; and the consolidated procurement calendar assembling every read from the track's eight modules.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Advanced buying: scope and structure
lessons.html:
This module completes the Procurement track: the instruments that manage supplier performance and repeat supply, the configuration register that governs the buying documents, and the consolidated calendar that assembles every read modules 1-7 defined. On completing this module you will be able to: build and read supplier scorecards with weighted criteria from document data; run the standings and their actions; conduct relationship reviews from measured evidence; operate buying-side blanket orders and distinguish them from rate arrangements; state the subcontracting flow and when it applies; maintain Buying Settings as control-register rows; and run the procurement function on its consolidated calendar.

Where this module sits. Modules 1-7 built the transaction machinery: the supplier register, the item's buying side, demand, the quotation cycle, the order, the receipt, and the match. Their documents accumulated measured facts at every step — confirmed dates against arrival dates, ordered quantities against counted quantities, agreed rates against claimed rates, claims against resolutions. This module is where those facts become management: the supplier relationship is managed from what the documents measured, and the conversations that shape next year's supply are conducted from this year's records.

The module's instruments.

1. Supplier scorecards (Chapters 2-3) — the weighted, periodic measurement of each supplier from document data, with standings that carry configured consequences.
2. Relationship reviews (Chapter 4) — the scheduled conversations, tiered by supplier importance, agenda'd from the scorecard and the files.
3. Blanket orders (Chapter 5) — committed-quantity agreements for repeat supply, called off as needed.
4. Subcontracting (Chapter 6) — supplying materials to a vendor and receiving finished goods, where the site's operations use it.
5. The control register and the calendar (Chapter 7) — the Buying Settings rows and the assembled reads.

Custody. The procurement function maintains scorecards and runs the calendar; review outcomes minute per the standing record rules; scorecard criteria and weights are policy decisions changed by decision with dates; and the standing rule: performance is measured from documents, standings carry stated consequences, and no supplier conversation of consequence happens without the file open.

Module contents. Chapter 2: scorecard structure. Chapter 3: standings and actions. Chapter 4: relationship reviews. Chapter 5: blanket orders. Chapter 6: subcontracting. Chapter 7: the control register and the calendar. Chapter 8: worked example. Chapter 9: review, the module rule, and the track close.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — Supplier scorecards: structure and weights
lessons.html:
The scorecard measures each supplier per period from document data. This chapter is its construction.

1. The Supplier Scorecard doctype. Open Supplier Scorecard (awesome bar) > New, per supplier: the evaluation period (monthly or quarterly per the policy), the weighted criteria, and the standings ladder (Chapter 3). The system evaluates each period automatically from the variables below, and the period scores accumulate into the supplier's running standing.

2. The criteria and the standing weights. Each criterion carries a weight; the weights sum to one hundred, and the standing policy sets them:

1. Price competitiveness — weight 40. The supplier's rates against the market evidence: the quotation cycles' comparisons (module 4), the trend read's movements against notice and market reference (module 2), and rate fidelity at the match (module 7). The heaviest weight because price is the largest lever on the landed cost the business sells against.
2. Delivery performance — weight 35. On-time-in-full from the receiving records (module 6): arrival dates against confirmed dates per drop, and quantity fidelity — short receipts and over-receipts against ordered rows. Measured per drop precisely because module 5's split rows made each drop its own commitment.
3. Quality — weight 25. The condition record: rejection rates by cause from the receipts, inspection failures from the quarantine lane, claim frequency and resolution conduct from the claims file.

3. The variables are document facts. Each criterion computes from the fields the track's documents captured: the scorecard is credible precisely because its inputs were recorded at the dock, on the orders, and in the match — not recalled at review time. A scorecard fed by impressions measures the loudest recent event; a scorecard fed by documents measures the year. Where a variable cannot compute from documents for a period (a supplier with no orders in the window), the period is marked as unmeasured rather than scored by assumption, and the standing carries forward on the measured periods.

4. Weight governance. The 40/35/25 structure is the standing policy for the core goods classes; classes may vary by decision (essential lines weighting delivery higher, per module 4's award criteria mirror), and any change is a dated policy decision recorded with the scorecard configuration — the same fields-move-by-decision rule as every register in the programme. The weights are reviewed annually with the policy, not adjusted to move a particular supplier's score.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Standings and actions
lessons.html:
Scores convert to standings, and standings carry consequences. This chapter is the ladder and its operation.

1. The standings ladder. The scorecard configuration maps score bands to standings, and each standing carries configured actions:

1. The healthy band — no restrictions: the relationship operates normally, and the score's trend is the review's material.
2. The warning band — the score triggers the flag: the supplier's next cycle participation and open orders continue, and the warning routes to the relationship review's agenda with the criterion that moved — a warning is a scheduled conversation, not a quiet note.
3. The restriction bands — the configured gates: prevent new Requests for Quotation, prevent new Purchase Orders — applied by the system at the configured standing. A supplier the business will not order from is a standing with a reason on file, not an informal understanding one buyer holds.

2. The actions are stated in advance. The ladder's structure means consequences are policy, applied evenly: the supplier at the restriction band is there by measured score, the standing is visible on their record, and the route back — the improvement the next periods must show — is arithmetic rather than persuasion. The evenness matters commercially: a supplier base that knows performance is measured and consequences are automatic negotiates differently from one that knows exceptions are available to whoever asks.

3. Overrides. The configured gate can be overridden where the policy permits — the sole-source supplier whose restriction would stop the business — by the named role, with the reason recorded and the item routed to the review: an override is a documented risk acceptance, and repeated overrides for one supplier are the concentration finding (module 1) restated as a performance finding.

4. The scorecard feeds the machinery.

1. The comparison worksheet (module 4) carries the scorecard figures in its performance columns — the award weighs measured history.
2. The review agenda (Chapter 4) opens with the standing and its movement.
3. The planning fields (module 2) draw lead-time reality from the delivery record.
4. The concentration and risk reads (module 1) read standings across the base: a critical class whose suppliers cluster in warning bands is a supply risk stated in advance.

5. The measured-conversation rule. Every performance conversation with a supplier cites the periods, the criteria, and the documents behind them. The rule works in both directions: the supplier who disputes a figure is answered from the receipts and the signed notes — and where the supplier is right, the correction is made and the score recomputes, because the scorecard's authority rests on its accuracy.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — Relationship reviews
lessons.html:
The scheduled conversations that manage the supplier base. This chapter is the cadence, the agenda, and the record.

1. The tiering. Reviews scale by supplier importance, per the policy:

1. The critical tier — the concentration suppliers and sole sources (module 1's risk read names them): quarterly reviews, attended at the relationship level.
2. The core tier — the standing arrangement suppliers: semi-annual reviews.
3. The transactional tier — annual file reviews, meeting only where the scorecard or the claims file raises cause.

2. The agenda, from the files. The review is prepared, not improvised — the agenda assembles from the track's records:

1. The scorecard — the standing, the period trend, the criterion movements (Chapter 3).
2. The claims and exceptions file — open claims by age, the quarter's matching exceptions by type (module 7's pattern), resolution conduct both ways.
3. Payment performance, both directions — the supplier's delivery against the business's payment timeliness (module 8 reads the module 7 aging honestly: the business's own overdue lines are on this agenda too, because the relationship's terms credibility is negotiated capital).
4. The commercial pipeline — arrangement validity and the re-quote calendar (module 4), volume trajectory against bands, the concentration position, and the coming year's structure.

3. The conduct. The measured-conversation rule governs: figures cited from documents, disputes resolved against records, and the improvement asks specific — the criterion, the target, the period. The review is also where the supplier's asks are heard on the same standard: their statement reconciliation items, their payment experience, their forecast needs — the file is opened in both directions because supply relationships that survive price cycles are built on mutual records, not mutual impressions.

4. The outcome minute. One page per review, filed with the supplier's record: the standing and trend as discussed, the commitments made each way (the improvement targets, the payment or forecast undertakings), the commercial decisions (renewal intentions, band adjustments routed to the module 4 governance), and the date of the next review. The minute is the continuity instrument — the next review opens by reading the last one's commitments against what the documents then measured — and the annual compilation of minutes per tier files with the procurement function's records for the owner's yearly read of the supply base.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Blanket orders
lessons.html:
Repeat supply can commit in advance. This chapter is the buying-side blanket order and its boundaries.

1. The instrument. The blanket order records a committed quantity of an item from a supplier at an agreed rate over a period — the buying mirror of the selling side's instrument. Individual Purchase Orders then call off against it: each call-off draws the blanket's rate, consumes its quantity, and runs the ordinary machinery (receipt, match, payment) as any order does.

2. Blanket order versus arrangement. The distinction from module 4's rate arrangements, stated precisely:

1. The arrangement holds agreed rates (or bands) with no quantity commitment — the business buys what it needs at the agreed price; the supplier holds the price for the validity.
2. The blanket order adds the quantity commitment — the business commits to the volume, and the rate reflects that commitment. The commitment is the price's consideration: a blanket rate is typically inside the arrangement band precisely because the supplier can plan production against committed volume.
3. The choice is a decision — commit volume where demand is stable and the rate improvement pays for the flexibility surrendered; hold to arrangements where demand varies. The consolidation history (module 3's worksheets across periods) is the evidence the choice reads.

3. The mechanics. The blanket order records supplier, item, committed quantity, rate, and period; call-off orders reference it and consume it; the remaining balance is visible on the record. The call-offs are ordinary orders in every other respect — scheduled per row, received at the dock, matched at the invoice — and the blanket's rate governs them as the arrangement's rate governs its purchases.

4. The consumption read — monthly. Committed quantity against called-off quantity against period elapsed: the trajectory states whether the commitment will be met. Under-consumption approaching period end is a commercial conversation held early — the shortfall's treatment per the agreement's terms (carry-over, rate adjustment, or settlement) is negotiated from the trajectory, not discovered at expiry. Over-consumption ahead of schedule is the renewal conversation arriving early, with the volume evidence in hand.

5. Expiry is a negotiation, never a rollover. The blanket's end date enters the re-quote calendar (module 4): renewal re-prices against the period's actual volumes, the scorecard's measured performance, and the market's movement — the same rule as every validity in the track, because a commitment renewed by inattention is a rate the market stopped testing.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Subcontracting
lessons.html:
Some operations send materials out and receive finished goods back. This chapter is the subcontracting flow.

1. What subcontracting is. The business supplies raw materials to a vendor; the vendor processes them; the business receives finished goods and pays a processing charge. The structure appears in retail-adjacent operations as repacking (bulk into retail packs), kitting and bundling at a co-packer, labelling and compliance marking, and light assembly — the vendor's service transforms stock the business already owns.

2. The document flow.

1. The subcontracting order — the Purchase Order flagged for subcontracting: the finished item, its quantity, and the service rate (the processing charge per unit) — the vendor is being bought a service, not goods.
2. The materials definition — the finished item's bill of materials states what raw materials each unit consumes: the components, their quantities, the expected consumption.
3. The material transfer — the raw materials move to the subcontractor's warehouse: a warehouse in the business's own tree (module 1 of the Inventory track) representing stock physically at the vendor — still the business's stock, on the business's books, visible to every stock read. The transfer documents what was sent, with identity where controlled.
4. The receipt — finished goods receive against the order per module 6's full discipline: counted, condition-split, identified. Posting consumes the raw materials from the subcontractor warehouse per the materials definition and brings the finished goods into stock.
5. The invoice and match — the vendor invoices the service charge; the match runs service-rate against order per module 7.

3. The valuation. The finished item's cost assembles from its parts: the consumed materials at their carried valuation plus the service charge — the landed-thinking rule (module 2) applied to processing: the shelf cost of the repacked unit includes what it cost to have it repacked.

4. The reconciliation reads. The subcontractor warehouse reconciles like any warehouse — the stock the books say is at the vendor against the vendor's own statement of holdings, per the counting rules — and the consumption reconciles per order: materials sent against materials consumed against finished goods received, with variances (process loss beyond the definition's allowance, unreturned excess) worked as claims per the standing procedures. Stock at vendors is stock at risk in a specific way: it is inventory the business cannot see daily, and the reconciliation cadence is the control.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The control register and the procurement calendar
lessons.html:
The buying documents run under configured controls, and the function runs on a calendar. This chapter closes both.

1. Buying Settings as control-register rows. Each setting is a policy decision with an owner and a reason, per the standing control-register pattern:

1. Purchase Order required — receipts and invoices require an order reference: the configuration that enforces module 3's standing rule (no purchase without its demand and commitment) and gives the match its first document. The exception role, where the site permits direct invoicing for defined classes (utilities, statutory payments), is named with its classes.
2. Purchase Receipt required — stock invoices require a receipt: the second document's guarantee, and the reason billed-not-received is an exception rather than a norm.
3. Maintain same rate through the cycle — the order's rate carries to receipt and invoice: the configuration behind module 6's untouched-rate rule and module 7's rate match, with variances routed to exceptions rather than absorbed.
4. Over-receipt tolerance — the dock's admission band (module 6), low, with the exception role named.
5. Supplier-item and identity defaults — the register behaviours the site standardises: naming series, default groups, the mandatory fields the gate enforces (module 1).

2. The settings read — quarterly. The register sampled against configuration; changes since last read reconciled to their decisions; the drift-versus-decision distinction maintained, per the programme's standing audit pattern.

3. The consolidated procurement calendar. The track's reads assembled by cadence — the function's operating rhythm:

1. Daily — the demand screen on its cadence (module 3); the dock's expected arrivals and receipts posted same-day (module 6); invoices entered and matched as they arrive (module 7).
2. Weekly — the reorder and consolidation window closing with orders submitted (modules 3, 5); the order book with incoming, overdue, and at-risk (module 5); received-not-billed and billed-not-received (modules 5, 7); open claims and clearing (modules 6-7); the exception queue and held invoices (module 7); the payment run on terms with the verified-account check (module 7); quotation cycles and validity (module 4); quarantine holds (module 6).
3. Monthly — buying price changes and completeness (module 2); the price trend read with the selling hand-off (module 2); bank-detail changes (module 1); the amendments read (module 5); the receipt audit and receiving-performance compilation (module 6); statement reconciliations (module 7); blanket consumption (module 5 of this chapter's numbering — Chapter 5); scorecard periods evaluating (Chapters 2-3).
4. Quarterly — the trace audit (module 3); response rates, award patterns, and the savings record (module 4); cancellations and closures (module 5); exception patterns (module 7); the settings read; relationship reviews per tier (Chapter 4); the concentration and risk read (module 1).
5. Annually — the register lifecycle review (module 1); the planning-field and policy reviews (module 2); re-quote cycles per class and arrangement renewals (module 4, Chapter 5); the scorecard weight review (Chapter 2); the supply-base compilation for the owner (Chapter 4).

4. The calendar's function. Every control in the track is a read someone runs on a date. The calendar assigns each to its owner and cadence, and the function's health is auditable in one question per read: when did it last run, and where are its findings filed.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Worked example: the Emzor year-one review
lessons.html:
This chapter closes the standing case: the first annual review of the arrangement modules 4-7 executed. Values and outcomes are listed per step.

Step 1 — the scorecard compiles (Chapters 2-3). Twelve months of document data evaluate under the 40/35/25 weights:

1. Price (40) — the band rate held through validity; one notified increase routed and absorbed into the selling review per module 2's hand-off; the trend read shows movement with notice against market reference: the criterion scores in the healthy band.
2. Delivery (35) — measured per drop across the year's orders: on-time-in-full at 91% — the misses documented on their orders with the chase-ladder records, none breaking cover into stock-out.
3. Quality (25) — the condition record: the year's rejection rate at 1.7% of received volume by cause (transit crush), claims resolved by replacement within agreed deadlines, no inspection failures, resolution conduct prompt. The weighted score lands Emzor in the healthy band, trend stable.

Step 2 — the agenda assembles (Chapter 4). The critical-tier quarterly review, year-end edition: the scorecard and trend; the claims file (all closed, the drop-one replacement's cross-references complete); the exception pattern (the single corrected-invoice pair, closed with documents); payment performance both ways — the business's runs on terms throughout, the terms credibility intact for the negotiation; the commercial pipeline — the arrangement expiring, actual annual volume against the band, and the concentration position with the second manufacturer's share performing.

Step 3 — the conversation runs measured (Chapters 3-4). The review cites periods and documents: the 91% delivery figure with its drop-level records; the damage cause raised with the packaging question (the transit-crush pattern routed to a packing change for the coming year — a specific ask with a criterion and a period); Emzor's own asks heard from their reconciliation file. The minute records the commitments each way.

Step 4 — the renewal prices from evidence (Chapters 4-5). The re-quote calendar owned the expiry: the renewal cycle runs per module 4 with the year's actual volumes as the comparison quantity, the scorecard in the performance columns, and the second manufacturer quoting the overlap. The outcome: the arrangement renews with the band structure adjusted to the measured volume trajectory, the packaging commitment written into terms, and the secondary share confirmed as the standing concentration mitigation. Separately, the consumables classes — stable-demand packing materials — convert from arrangement to blanket order on the consumption evidence: committed volume for a rate inside the band, the trade stated in the decision minute.

Step 5 — the calendar carries it (Chapter 7). The renewal's validity enters the re-quote calendar; the blanket's consumption read starts its monthly cadence; the scorecard rolls into year two measuring the packaging commitment; the next review is dated in the minute.

The track's evidence, complete. One supplier file now demonstrates the whole track: the verified register entry, the sourced rates, the traced demand, the cycle's minutes, the committed order, the signed dock records, the matched invoices, the reconciled statements, the measured scorecard, and the review minute that prices year two — every figure in the conversation answerable to a document in one lookup.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common errors, the module rule, and the track close
lessons.html:
The errors that recur in supplier management, each with its correction and prevention — then the track's close.

Error 1 — the impression scorecard. Symptom: supplier standing set by the loudest recent event; scores adjusted to justify decided outcomes; the base learning that measurement is negotiable. Correction: scores recomputed from documents. Prevention: criteria computing from document variables, and weights changed only by dated policy decision.

Error 2 — the warning nobody schedules. Symptom: standings fall into warning bands with no conversation following; the restriction gate arriving as a surprise; the improvement route never stated. Correction: the warned suppliers routed to reviews. Prevention: the warning band's action — a scheduled conversation with the criterion named.

Error 3 — the standing exception habit. Symptom: restriction gates overridden routinely for the same suppliers; the ladder's evenness gone; measured consequences replaced by asking. Correction: overrides compiled and routed to the risk review. Prevention: overrides by named role with reasons, and repeated overrides read as concentration findings.

Error 4 — the blanket rollover. Symptom: committed-quantity agreements renewed by inattention at stale rates; consumption never read; shortfalls discovered at expiry. Correction: the renewal re-priced from actuals. Prevention: the monthly consumption read and expiry on the re-quote calendar.

Error 5 — invisible stock at vendors. Symptom: materials at subcontractors untracked or written off informally; consumption variances unworked; the vendor's holdings unreconciled. Correction: the subcontractor warehouse reconciled and variances claimed. Prevention: vendor stock as a warehouse the reads see, on the counting calendar.

Error 6 — the calendar that exists on paper. Symptom: reads defined but unrun; findings unfiled; controls present in the manual and absent in the month. Correction: the calendar re-owned read by read. Prevention: each read with an owner and a date, auditable by the one question — when did it last run, and where are its findings.

Review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: build scorecards on the 40/35/25 weights from document variables; operate the standings ladder with stated actions and documented overrides; run tiered reviews from assembled agendas to outcome minutes; distinguish blanket orders from arrangements and read consumption; state the subcontracting flow with vendor-warehouse stock and assembled valuation; maintain the Buying Settings register; and run the consolidated calendar.

Module rule 8: the supplier base is managed from documents — performance measured on weighted criteria the papers recorded, standings carrying stated consequences applied evenly, reviews conducted from files to minutes, commitments priced from actual volumes, and every read on a calendar with an owner.

The track close. Eight modules built one continuous machine: the verified register (1), the costed item (2), the recorded demand (3), the evidenced rate (4), the committed order (5), the counted arrival (6), the matched claim (7), and the measured relationship (8). The standing case ran through all eight — from Emzor's registration to the 300-carton order, the 177-and-3 dock split, the corrected invoice, and the year-one review that priced year two. The Procurement track is complete.
